findings.title: html_report's compare fingerprint reimplements (and regresses) synthesize's already-fixed finding-identity logic
findings.description: synthesize.finding_fingerprint() (synthesize.py lines 515-534) deliberately excludes free-text `description` from its stable-identity hash, with the comment 'free-text description... agent prose is re-worded every run' — and the result is stored on every finding as f["fingerprint"] by build_report(). Separately, html_report.py's _fingerprint(), used exclusively by the --compare feature's _match_findings(), computes its own independent hash from [panel, category, file, title, description] — including the exact raw description text that synthesize's version was fixed to exclude for this precise reason — and never reads the already-computed finding.get("fingerprint") field that ships in every synthesized report.
findings.impact: synthesize.py --compare loads two already-synthesized report JSON files (each containing the correct, stable fingerprint per finding) but _match_findings() ignores that field and recomputes its own, reintroducing the non-determinism bug that finding_fingerprint() was written to solve. Any agent-sourced finding whose description is reworded between two runs of the same underlying issue will fingerprint differently in the compare view, and _match_findings() will report it as one 'resolved' entry plus one unrelated 'new' entry instead of 'unchanged' — corrupting exactly the delta counts and per-finding delta badges that --compare exists to produce.
findings.remediation: Have html_report._fingerprint() prefer the precomputed finding.get("fingerprint") (falling back to a local computation only for legacy reports that predate the field, and dropping description from that fallback to match synthesize.finding_fingerprint's rule_id/title discriminator).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion checks out against the code. (1) /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/html_report.py lines 246-257 define `_fingerprint(finding)` whose payload is `[panel, category, _normalize_path(location.file), title, description]` — the raw free-text `description` is part of the identity hash. (2) /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/synthesize.py lines 531-552 define `finding_fingerprint()` with the explicit docstring 'Deliberately EXCLUDES line numbers (issues survive code moves) and free-text description (agent prose is re-worded every run)', and uses a rule_id-or-title discriminator gated on tool-sourcing. (3) build_report() sets the result on every finding: synthesize.py line 641 `f["fingerprint"] = finding_fingerprint(f)`; tests/test_synthesize.py:1599-1602 assert the field ships on report findings, and the current artifact docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-self-scan-report.json carries 73 `"fingerprint"` values. (4) html_report never reads that field: grep for `fingerprint` in html_report.py returns only `_fingerprint` (246), its two call sites in `_match_findings` (269, 272) and the match-dict key (284-288); `finding.get("fingerprint")` appears nowhere. (5) The compare path does load already-synthesized JSON: synthesize.py lines 879-903 json.load both files and hand them to `html_report.write_html(report_b, html_out, compare_report=report_a)`, which reaches `render()` -> `_match_findings()` (html_report.py 683-692). So two reports each carrying the stable fingerprint are matched by a second, description-sensitive hash, and any prose rewording of the same underlying issue yields one 'resolved' + one 'new' instead of 'unchanged', skewing the delta cards in `_render_compare_dashboard` and the per-card `delta-badge`. Two caveats the auditor should carry forward, neither of which refutes the claim: (a) the current behaviour is test-encoded — tests/test_html_report.py:336-347 ('changed_not_fixed') deliberately mutates only `description` and asserts new=1/resolved=1, with the comment 'Modify the description so the SHA fingerprint changes', and the original design spec docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-html-report-design.md:97 specifies the description-inclusive hash — so a fix must update that test and the spec, not just the function; (b) the remediation's suggested legacy fallback is genuinely needed: docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-self-scan-report.json contains zero `"fingerprint"` keys, so pre-field reports can still be fed to --compare. On severity, the blast radius is confined to the --compare HTML view (no effect on the JSON report, grades, or the gate), so MEDIUM is on the generous side, but the divergence and its described effect are real.

findings.title: Ad hoc sys.path bootstrap duplicated verbatim across three entry-point scripts
findings.description: synthesize.py (lines 13-18), run_tools.py (lines 11-13), and _run_adapter.py (lines 10-12) each independently execute `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))` immediately before `import scripts.<module>`, so that the `scripts` package resolves regardless of CWD. The same two-line idiom is copy-pasted three times rather than factored into one shared helper, and it hard-codes an assumption that each file lives exactly two directories below the importable root.
findings.impact: There is no single source of truth for how these scripts locate the `scripts` package; a future move of any one file (or a switch to installing skill/ as a real package) silently breaks that file's imports with a bare ModuleNotFoundError and no indication of the expected layout, and any layout fix must be applied in three places kept in sync by hand.
findings.remediation: Factor the bootstrap into one shared module (e.g. skill/scripts/_bootstrap.py) imported first by every entry point, or eliminate it by shipping skill/ as an installable package with `scripts` as a proper package.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: All three cited sites exist at the cited lines and the bootstrap line is byte-for-byte identical in each: synthesize.py:13, run_tools.py:11, and _run_adapter.py:10 each contain `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))`, immediately followed by `import scripts.<module>` statements (synthesize.py:14-18, run_tools.py:12-13, _run_adapter.py:12). The cited line ranges are accurate. I confirmed no shared helper exists: a grep for `_bootstrap|bootstrap|PYTHONPATH` across /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill returns no matches, and skill/scripts/ contains no bootstrap module (file listing: _run_adapter, citations, depth_planner, orchestrator, provenance, model_resolver, run_fixture_tests, ingest_tools, run_tools, dispatch, evidence, html_report, synthesize). The 'no single source of truth' impact is stronger than the claim states, in two ways I verified independently. First, there is a fourth, DIVERGENT variant: skill/scripts/dispatch.py:9 uses `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))` (one dirname, not two) and then imports bare `depth_planner`/`model_resolver` (lines 10-11), while skill/scripts/tools/base.py:9 uses yet another form (`os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir, os.pardir)`) — so the same problem is already solved three different ways in-tree. Second, skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py does `from scripts.tools.sarif_utils import (...)` at line 13 with NO bootstrap of its own, so it silently depends on whichever caller mutated sys.path first. On the remediation's feasibility: pyproject.toml has project metadata and ruff config only — no [build-system] and no package/tool discovery table — so the repo is not pip-installable today and the sys.path mutation really is the only import mechanism; there is also no skill/scripts/__init__.py (only skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py), so `scripts` resolves as a PEP 420 namespace package. The minor imprecision that the assumption is 'each file lives exactly two directories below the importable root' (the files are at <root>/scripts/<file>.py, i.e. two path components below root, one directory below) does not affect the substance. CWE-710 (Improper Adherence to Coding Standards) is a reasonable class fit. LOW severity is appropriate: this is a maintainability/duplication issue, not a correctness or security bug — the code works today under all three entry points.

findings.title: Large monolithic synthesize.py file (980+ lines)
findings.description: synthesize.py is a large monolithic module with approximately 980 lines, containing many helper functions with underscore prefixes (_sev_rank, _conf_rank, _is_tool_sourced, etc.). The file combines multiple concerns: finding normalization, deduplication, citation enrichment, report building, and CLI orchestration.
findings.impact: Large files reduce maintainability, make testing harder, increase cognitive load, and increase regression risk when modifications are made.
findings.remediation: Refactor synthesize.py into smaller focused modules: finding_normalization.py, finding_deduplication.py, report_builder.py, cli.py.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The size claim is accurate: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/synthesize.py is 998 lines (line-count grep; the file's last statement is `sys.exit(main())` at line 998), matching '980+ lines'. The three named helpers all exist with the underscore-prefixed convention described: _sev_rank at line 137, _conf_rank at 144, _is_tool_sourced at 152; a full top-level def grep returns 33 module-level functions. The mixed-concerns characterization holds and is if anything understated — in one module: normalization (normalize_finding:47, load_findings:96), deduplication and cross-panel merge (dedupe:229, _reinforce_merge:205, cross_panel_corroboration:332), tool-finding aggregation and policy derivation (aggregate_tool_findings:555, tool_rule_id:514, derive_tool_policy_mode:491), grading and CI gating (grade:409, risk_level:422, gate_verdict:430, severity_stats:444), report construction (build_report:604), schema validation (validate_report:716, attach_schema_status:705), summary rendering and artifact writing (render_summary:758, write_report:812, _derive_html_path:835), and full CLI orchestration (main:841, ~155 lines with 17 argparse options and a separate --compare code path). One small overstatement I should flag: 'citation enrichment' is NOT implemented here — synthesize.py only calls into scripts/citations.py (citations.enrich_citations at lines 638 and 942), so that concern is already factored out; the same is true of evidence handling (delegated to scripts/evidence.py) and HTML (scripts/html_report.py). That does not change the verdict, since the remaining concerns listed above are genuinely co-located. Judgment context the auditor should weigh: this is a subjective maintainability threshold, not a defect — the project is deliberately stdlib-only, ruff is configured with only E/F/W (no complexity or file-length rules), CONTRIBUTING.md sets no module-size policy, and the module already delegates four major subsystems to sibling modules, so the author is clearly splitting along some boundary already. The attached CWE-1104 (Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components) is inapplicable; CWE-1121 (Excessive McCabe Cyclomatic Complexity) / the CWE-1120 'Excessive Code Complexity' family is the correct class. Confirmed as a LOW-severity, correctly-scoped maintainability observation.

findings.title: Large embedded CSS and JS in html_report.py
findings.description: html_report.py embeds CSS (~113 lines, lines 8-120) and JavaScript (~48 lines, lines 122-169) as module-level string constants. These should ideally be in separate files or generated by a template engine. The embedding makes the Python code harder to edit and prevents syntax highlighting/linting of CSS/JS.
findings.impact: Reduces maintainability and developer experience. CSS and JS cannot be linted or syntax-highlighted when embedded in Python strings.
findings.remediation: Extract CSS to style.css and JS to script.js, or use a template engine. If embedding is necessary, add length comments marking sections.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The measurements are correct. In /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/html_report.py, `_CSS` opens at line 8 and closes at 120 (111 lines of stylesheet), `_JS` opens at 122 and closes at 169 (46 lines of script), and both are module-level triple-quoted string constants interpolated by `_html_doc()` at lines 185 and 191. So 'CSS ~113 lines (8-120), JS ~48 lines (122-169), embedded as module-level string constants' is an accurate description of the file, and the consequence — no CSS/JS syntax highlighting or linting inside Python string literals — follows directly. I confirm the observation but the auditor should weigh three mitigating facts before acting on the remediation as written. (1) The inlining is a deliberate, documented constraint, not an oversight: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-html-report-design.md lines 11-14 require 'Vanilla HTML/CSS/JS only — no frameworks, no CDNs, no external dependencies', 'Self-contained artifact — one .html file with all CSS and JS inlined', and 'Zero new Python dependencies — the renderer is stdlib-only', and line 23-24 name `_CSS` and `_JS` as intended module members. The 'template engine' half of the remediation directly contradicts the zero-dependency constraint. (2) Splitting into sibling style.css/script.js is architecturally possible — skill/reference/ already ships non-Python assets (cwe-catalog.json, model-profiles.yml, report-schema.json) — but it converts a stdlib-only pure-function renderer into one with runtime file I/O and path resolution, which is a real trade, not a free win. (3) The cited CWE-1104 ('Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components') has no bearing on embedded CSS/JS strings and should be dropped as a miscitation; I could not verify any CWE that fits. LOW severity is right; this is a developer-experience preference with no functional or security consequence.

findings.title: Helper name _depth_gte computes the inverse relation of what its name promises
findings.description: `_depth_gte(lens_depth, panel_depth)` reads as "lens_depth >= panel_depth" but its body returns `DEPTH_RANK.get(lens_depth, 0) <= DEPTH_RANK.get(panel_depth, 0)` — a <= comparison of the two ranks in that argument order. The call site (`plan_lenses`, `if not _depth_gte(threshold, depth): continue`) relies on this inverted meaning to implement the documented rule "lens.depth_threshold <= profile.depth", so the code is functionally correct today, but the identifier actively misleads about the comparison direction.
findings.impact: A maintainer reading or reusing this helper elsewhere is likely to assume it means "first arg is at least as deep as second arg" and pass arguments in the wrong order, silently breaking lens-spawn depth gating.
findings.remediation: Rename to something that matches the body's actual semantics, e.g. `_threshold_met(threshold_depth, actual_depth)`, or invert the body to match `_gte` and swap the call-site argument order; add a one-line docstring stating the comparison direction explicitly.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified verbatim at skill/scripts/depth_planner.py:8-9: `def _depth_gte(lens_depth, panel_depth): return DEPTH_RANK.get(lens_depth, 0) <= DEPTH_RANK.get(panel_depth, 0)`. The identifier suffix `gte` under the conventional reading of `f(a, b)` promises `a >= b`, but the body computes `rank(a) <= rank(b)`. There is no docstring to disambiguate. The sole call site (depth_planner.py:32, `if not _depth_gte(threshold, depth): continue`, with `threshold = lens.get('depth_threshold', 'standard')` at line 31 and `depth = profile.get('depth', 'standard')` at line 22) depends on the inverted meaning to implement the rule documented in the plan_lenses docstring at line 18 ('lens.depth_threshold <= profile.depth'). So the behavior is correct today — I traced the test expectations in tests/test_depth_planner.py (shallow profile spawns only the shallow-threshold 'structure' lens; deep profile spawns known_vulns/injection/novel), which match `threshold <= depth`, i.e. the `<=` body, not a literal `>=` reading of the name. The claim is therefore accurate on both counts: functionally correct, but the name states the inverse relation of the body. Grep confirms `_depth_gte` has exactly one definition and one call site in live code (other hits are prior scan reports and the design plan doc), so no caller is currently mis-invoking it; the risk is prospective, consistent with the LOW severity and 'style' category. Note also that .panopticon.prev-20260803/findings-._5-code-panel_review.json already carries an equivalent prior-run finding ('Misleading helper name _depth_gte actually computes lens_depth <= panel_depth'), i.e. this is an unfixed repeat observation, not a new regression. CWE-1099 (inconsistent naming) is a loose but defensible fit; I did not verify it against the CWE catalog text.

findings.title: Bare except Exception blocks in orchestrator.py omit the codebase's noqa:BLE001 tolerant-by-design convention
findings.description: `collect_changed_files` has four intentionally-broad `except Exception:` blocks (lines 136, 145, 157, 169) that swallow git subprocess failures with no stderr diagnostic and no lint-suppression comment, and `load_catalog` has a fifth at line 303 (`except Exception as e:`) that does log but still lacks the annotation. Every sibling module in skill/scripts/ (citations.py:170,266; ingest_tools.py:80; synthesize.py:109; run_tools.py:43,147,179; tools/cargo_audit.py:39; tools/sarif_utils.py:113) marks the same intentional-tolerance pattern with `# noqa: BLE001` plus a short rationale.
findings.impact: Inconsistent lint-suppression annotation makes it unclear (to both readers and any future BLE001-enabled lint pass) whether these five broad excepts are deliberate tolerance or accidental over-catching, and the four unlogged ones in collect_changed_files also silently discard the underlying git error with no stderr trace.
findings.remediation: Add `# noqa: BLE001 - tolerant by design` (or equivalent) to all five sites, and add a stderr diagnostic to the four currently-silent ones in collect_changed_files, matching the convention used elsewhere in the package.

findings.title: Filename orchestrator.py collides with the unrelated 'orchestrator' concept used throughout the pipeline docs
findings.description: This module's own docstring and CLI describe it as a target/group resolver ("Resolve panopticon targets (files, dirs, groups, repos) to grouped file lists"; `ArgumentParser(description="panopticon target resolver")`), and SKILL.md invokes it as `python3 scripts/orchestrator.py` in the Discovery step. Elsewhere in the same docs (SKILL.md steps 6/8, agents/panel-review.md, agents/lens-sweep.md) "the orchestrator" refers to the top-level driving agent that dispatches subagents and writes their output files — a completely different concept from this script.
findings.impact: A contributor grepping the docs/codebase for "orchestrator" logic will be misdirected to this target-resolver script instead of the actual pipeline-driving agent behavior, adding friction when tracing the pipeline.
findings.remediation: Rename the module to something reflecting its actual role (e.g. target_resolver.py or resolve_targets.py), or note in its docstring that it is unrelated to "the orchestrator" agent role used elsewhere.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual element checks out. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/orchestrator.py:2-3 docstring reads 'Resolve panopticon targets (files, dirs, groups, repos) to grouped file lists', and line 479 is `ArgumentParser(description="panopticon target resolver")` — the module is purely a target/group resolver (main() only dispatches on --group/--directory/--file/--files/--changes/--repo-scan and emits JSON; it never dispatches subagents). Meanwhile 'the orchestrator' denotes the driving agent elsewhere: skill/SKILL.md:43 ('the orchestrator writes it to .panopticon/scout-{group}.json'), :51 ('the orchestrator writes it to the entry's out_file'), :60 ('Advisors are read-only; the orchestrator performs the write'), skill/agents/panel-review.md:17 and skill/agents/lens-sweep.md:17 (both: 'you cannot write files; the orchestrator writes your findings to {out_file}'). SKILL.md:42 invokes the script in the Discovery step exactly as claimed. There is no skill/agents/orchestrator.md — the agent set is advisor/lens-sweep/panel-review/scout — so the word has no owning file and resolves to this script when grepped. The docstring carries no disambiguating note. README.md:78 even compounds it by listing 'orchestrator' among skill/scripts/ modules. This is a genuine naming collision, correctly filed as INFO/style with no functional impact; the cheapest fix is the docstring note rather than a rename, since SKILL.md:42, DEVELOPMENT.md:24 and DEVELOPMENT.md:134 all reference the path or module name.

findings.title: run_adapters uses f-strings while the rest of run_tools.py uses %-formatting for identical diagnostics
findings.description: `run_adapters` (lines 94-112) builds paths and stderr messages with f-strings (`f"{name}.{ext}"` at 101, `f"adapter {name} exited {rc}; skipping"` at 105, `f"adapter {name} failed: {e}; skipping"` at 111), while the structurally near-identical logic in `run_tools` (lines 115-181) and `main` use `%`-style formatting exclusively for the same category of message (e.g. `"tool %s exited %s; skipping%s" % (...)` at 138, `"adapter %s failed: %s; skipping" % (tool, e)` at 180-181). Every other reviewed script in skill/scripts/ (citations.py, evidence.py, dispatch.py, orchestrator.py, ingest_tools.py, model_resolver.py, synthesize.py) is internally consistent on %-formatting.
findings.impact: Purely cosmetic, but the mixed convention within one file (compounded by run_adapters appearing to be unused/superseded by run_tools's adapter-dispatch branch) signals leftover code from a different authoring pass and adds noise when diffing/reviewing this file.
findings.remediation: Normalize run_adapters (or remove it if superseded by run_tools's adapter dispatch path) to the file's dominant %-formatting style.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Every specific line cited checks out in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/run_tools.py. `run_adapters` uses f-strings at line 101 (`os.path.join(out_dir, f"{name}.{ext}")`), 105 (`f"adapter {name} exited {rc}; skipping"`) and 111 (`f"adapter {name} failed: {e}; skipping"`). The structurally parallel code elsewhere in the same file uses %-formatting exclusively: line 129 `"%s.sarif" % tool`, 131, 138-140 `"tool %s exited %s; skipping%s" % (...)`, 146, 148, 155 `"%s.%s" % (tool, ext)`, 165-166, 172 `"adapter %s exited %s; skipping" % (tool, res.returncode)`, 178, 180-181 `"adapter %s failed: %s; skipping" % (tool, e)`. Lines 172 and 180 are literally the same two messages as 105 and 111 in the other style, so the inconsistency is intra-file and message-for-message.

I also checked the claim's supporting assertion about sibling scripts: grepping for interpolating f-strings (pattern requiring an `{` inside the literal) across citations.py, evidence.py, dispatch.py, orchestrator.py, ingest_tools.py, model_resolver.py and synthesize.py returns zero matches — those seven files are indeed %-only, as stated.

The claim's parenthetical that `run_adapters` looks unused/superseded also holds: repo-wide grep for `run_adapters` finds only the definition, tests/test_run_tools.py:97, and docs; `main` at lines 193-204 calls `run_tools`, whose lines 152-180 duplicate the adapter dispatch.

One caveat for the auditor: the claim's implied 'repo convention is %-formatting' is only true of the seven files it names. skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py:21,26,32 emits the same 'adapter {name} ... skipping' messages with f-strings, and provenance.py, html_report.py and skill/scripts/tools/*.py use f-strings pervasively. There is no repo-wide linter enforcing either style (pyproject.toml sets ruff `select = ["E", "F", "W"]`). So this is a genuine within-file inconsistency but not a violation of any enforced standard — consistent with the LOW severity assigned.

findings.title: Partial, inconsistent PEP 484 type-hint adoption in run_tools.py
findings.description: `select_adapters(target: str, adapters: dict | None = None) -> dict:` (line 88) and `run_adapters(adapters: dict, target: str, out_dir: str, runner=None) -> list[str]:` (line 94) carry type hints, while every other function in the same file — `docker_available`, `detect_languages`, `select_tools`, `run_tools`, `main` — has none, and the file has no `from __future__ import annotations` import despite using `dict | None` union syntax that other untyped sibling modules avoid entirely.
findings.impact: Inconsistent typing within one module reduces the value of the hints that are present (readers can't rely on the file being type-checkable end to end) and signals the two typed functions were written in a separate pass from the rest.
findings.remediation: Either annotate the remaining public functions for consistency, or drop the two partial annotations to match the rest of the largely-untyped skill/scripts/ package.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The core observation is verifiable and accurate. In /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/run_tools.py, only two functions carry annotations: line 88 `def select_adapters(target: str, adapters: dict | None = None) -> dict:` and line 94 `def run_adapters(adapters: dict, target: str, out_dir: str, runner=None) -> list[str]:` (note `runner` is itself unannotated even in the typed pair). The other module-level functions — `docker_available` (36), `detect_languages` (54), `select_tools` (76), `run_tools` (115) — have no annotations at all. The module's imports are only `os`, `subprocess`, `sys` (lines 7-9), so there is indeed no `from __future__ import annotations`, while `dict | None` PEP 604 syntax is used at line 88. Two inaccuracies in the claim, neither fatal to it: (1) there is no `main` function in run_tools.py — the CLI lives in a bare `if __name__ == "__main__":` block at lines 184-205, so listing `main` among the unannotated functions is wrong; (2) the framing that this file sits in a 'largely-untyped skill/scripts/ package' whose siblings 'avoid [union syntax] entirely' is misleading — the entire skill/scripts/tools/ package plus provenance.py and run_fixture_tests.py are fully annotated AND each opens with `from __future__ import annotations` (e.g. tools/base.py:2 with `normalize_severity(value: str | None) -> str`, provenance.py:2 with `tool_provenance(adapter_name: str, reasoning: str | None = None) -> dict`). If anything that strengthens the inconsistency observation while weakening the claim's proposed 'drop the annotations' remediation. There is no correctness risk: pyproject.toml sets `requires-python = ">=3.11"` and `[tool.ruff] target-version = "py311"`, so `dict | None` evaluates fine at def-time without the future import, and ruff's lint select is `["E", "F", "W"]` with no ANN rules, so nothing enforces annotation completeness. Confirmed strictly as the INFO-severity cosmetic inconsistency it is claimed to be.

findings.title: run_adapters' broad except lacks the noqa:BLE001 annotation used elsewhere in the very same file
findings.description: `run_adapters`'s `except Exception as e:` at line 110 has no lint-suppression comment, while the three other intentionally-broad excepts in this same file (`docker_available` line 43, `run_tools` lines 147 and 179) are all annotated `# noqa: BLE001`.
findings.impact: Inconsistent within a single file; makes it ambiguous whether the line-110 catch is deliberate tolerance (matching the rest of the file's pattern) or an oversight.
findings.remediation: Add `# noqa: BLE001` (with rationale) to line 110 to match the file's established convention, or fold run_adapters into run_tools's already-annotated adapter-dispatch path.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Verified line by line in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/run_tools.py. A grep for `except Exception` in that file returns exactly four hits: line 43 `except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001`, line 110 `except Exception as e:` (no comment), line 147 `except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001`, line 179 `except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001`. So line 110 is the sole unannotated broad except in a file where the other three are annotated, exactly as claimed. All four catches are semantically the same 'tolerate and keep going' pattern (110 prints 'adapter %s failed; skipping' and continues the loop; 179 prints the identical message from the duplicate dispatch path), so the omission is an inconsistency rather than a signal of different intent.

Two pieces of context the auditor should have, neither of which falsifies the claim:
(1) The `# noqa: BLE001` markers are currently inert. pyproject.toml sets `[tool.ruff.lint] select = ["E", "F", "W"]`, and BLE001 (flake8-blind-except) is not in that set, nor is RUF100 (unused-noqa) enabled. Adding or omitting the comment changes no lint outcome today; the value is purely documentary intent-signalling, which matches the LOW severity.
(2) The convention is file-local, not repo-wide: skill/scripts/orchestrator.py has five unannotated broad excepts (lines 136, 145, 157, 169, 303), while synthesize.py:109, ingest_tools.py:80, citations.py:170,266, _run_adapter.py:25,31, tools/cargo_audit.py:39 and tools/sarif_utils.py:113 are annotated. The claim scopes its assertion to 'the very same file', which is precisely accurate.
CWE-1078 is a reasonable quality-measure mapping for source-style inconsistency; it is carried as verified:false and adds no weight either way.

findings.title: Exception handling in run_adapters never tested
findings.description: Lines 110-111 in run_tools.py contain exception handling for adapter.invoke() failures, but no test case exercises this path. The try-except block catches exceptions but test_run_adapters_writes_raw_output (line 89 in test_run_tools.py) only tests the success case.
findings.impact: Uncaught bugs in adapter exception handling would not be detected by tests.
findings.remediation: Add test case that mocks adapter.invoke() to raise an exception and verify run_adapters handles it gracefully.
references: skill/scripts/run_tools.py:94-112 (run_adapters, untested except at 110-111 and untested rc-skip at 104-106)
skill/scripts/run_tools.py:152-181 (the adapter path actually used in production, which is tested)

A repo-wide grep for `run_adapters` returns exactly one call site outside the definition and the design docs: tests/test_run_tools.py:97 inside test_run_adapters_writes_raw_output, whose FakeAdapter.invoke returns (b'{"results":[]}', 0) and cannot raise. No other test file in tests/ (full listing enumerated) references run_adapters, so lines 110-111 are unreachable by the suite. Adjacent tests that superficially look like coverage are not: test_run_tools_continues_after_one_tool_fails (tests/test_run_tools.py:71) exercises run_tools' except at line 148, and test_main_skips_adapter_that_crashes (:198) exercises _run_adapter.py's except at line 25 — different functions. findings.title: load_findings mixes four different stderr diagnostic-prefix conventions in a dozen lines
findings.description: Within `load_findings` alone: line 104 uses an unprefixed all-caps tag (`"MISSING: %s"`), line 110 uses a different unprefixed all-caps tag (`"PARSE ERROR %s: %s"`), lines 113 and 117 have no tag at all (`"not a JSON object: %s"`, `"no findings list in %s"`), and lines 127-128 use the module-name-lowercase-prefix convention (`"synthesize: stripped self-asserted %r from %s in %s"`) that the rest of the file (lines 613-614, 915-917, 948-949) and sibling modules (citations.py `"citations: ..."`, ingest_tools.py `"ingest: ..."`, dispatch.py `"dispatch: ..."`, evidence.py `"evidence: ..."`) use consistently. `validate_report`'s warnings/errors (lines 963, 965) add yet a fifth convention (`"WARN: %s"`, `"SCHEMA: %s"`).
findings.impact: Inconsistent, hard-to-grep stderr output makes it harder to filter synthesize.py's own diagnostics from a run's combined log (no single prefix to search for), and obscures which messages are this module's own vs. generic.
findings.remediation: Standardize all of load_findings' and validate_report's stderr prints on the module's own `"synthesize: <message>"` prefix convention already used elsewhere in the same file.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The cited location and its content match exactly. In /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/synthesize.py, `load_findings` spans lines 96-134 and contains, verbatim: line 104 `print("MISSING: %s" % path, file=sys.stderr)`; line 110 `print("PARSE ERROR %s: %s" % (path, e), ...)`; line 113 `print("not a JSON object: %s" % path, ...)`; line 117 `print("no findings list in %s" % path, ...)`; line 123 `print("skipping non-object finding in %s" % path, ...)` (a fifth, untagged message the claim omits); and lines 127-128 `print("synthesize: stripped self-asserted %r from %s in %s" ...)`. So within ~25 lines the module emits bare all-caps tags, untagged sentences, and the module-name prefix — the claim's substance holds. The module-prefix convention it points to is real elsewhere in the file (lines 631, 635, 920, 922, 933, 966 all begin `synthesize: `), and the competing conventions it names also exist: `WARN: %s` and `SCHEMA: %s` at lines 981 and 983 (plus an `ERROR: ` family at 885, 888, 894, 897, 901 that the claim does not mention). Two caveats that do not overturn it: (a) the supporting line numbers have drifted — the claim cites 613-614/915-917/948-949 for `synthesize: ` prints (613-614 is actually inside build_report's docstring) and 963/965 for WARN/SCHEMA (actually 981/983), and the WARN/SCHEMA prints live in `main`, not inside `validate_report`, which only returns the (errors, warnings) tuple; (b) the sibling-module 'consistently' claim is overstated — dispatch.py (373-434) and evidence.py (190-218) are consistent, but ingest_tools.py uses four variants (`ingest skip`, `ingest note`, `ingest error`, `ingest: ` at lines 60, 66, 75, 81, 94) and citations.py mixes `citations: ` (45) with `citation enrich error (finding %s)` (267). Every one of those corrections makes the underlying inconsistency broader, not narrower. The cited primary range (104-128) is exact, the impact (no single greppable prefix for this module's diagnostics in a combined run log) follows directly, and the remediation is coherent. Cosmetic only — no behavior depends on these strings; LOW/INFO is the right ceiling.

findings.title: Hardcoded User-Agent version string is stale relative to the project's actual current version
findings.description: `epss_lookup` hardcodes `"User-Agent": "panopticon/3.0.0"` (line 153). The project's actual current version is 4.2.0 elsewhere in this same codebase: SKILL.md's frontmatter `version: "4.2.0"`, synthesize.py's report `meta.version` (line 664, `"4.2.0"`), and evidence.py's verify-queue `version` (line 126, `"4.2.0"`). pyproject.toml's `[project].version` is also `3.0.0`, so this literal was likely copied from there and never updated as the two drifted.
findings.impact: The User-Agent sent to api.first.org misreports the running panopticon version, which is a minor correctness/observability issue on the API-consumer side, but its root cause is a stale hardcoded literal that should track the package's real version — a single-source-of-truth violation.
findings.remediation: Derive the User-Agent version from a single source of truth (e.g. read `pyproject.toml`'s `[project].version` or a shared `__version__`, and reconcile it with SKILL.md's 4.2.0) instead of a second hardcoded literal.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual element checks out except one line number. skill/scripts/citations.py:153 is literally `req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "panopticon/3.0.0"})`. The competing version literals are real: skill/SKILL.md:14 `version: "4.2.0"`, skill/scripts/evidence.py:126 `"version": "4.2.0"` in the verify-queue payload, and the report meta version in synthesize.py — which is at line 682, not line 664 as the claim states (line 664 is unrelated panel-grouping code). Three separate tests pin 4.2.0 as the user-visible version (tests/test_synthesize.py:1194 and :1479, tests/test_schema.py:170, tests/test_verify_queue.py:115). pyproject.toml:3 is indeed `version = "3.0.0"`, which supports the claim's own reading that the User-Agent literal was copied from packaging metadata and then drifted. There is no `__version__` or shared VERSION constant anywhere in the repo (grep for `__version__|VERSION` across .py files returns only unrelated KIMI_CODE_VERSION env handling in dispatch.py), confirming the single-source-of-truth violation: four independent hardcoded version literals across pyproject.toml, SKILL.md, synthesize.py, evidence.py, plus this one. The impact framing is fairly stated and appropriately LOW — this is an outbound informational header to api.first.org with no security or functional consequence. One practical detail the remediation omits: tests/test_citations.py:167 asserts `holder['req'].get_header('User-agent') == 'panopticon/3.0.0'`, so that test pins the stale value and must be updated alongside any fix. Strictly, the claim's phrase 'stale relative to the project's actual current version' is slightly overstated since the UA exactly matches pyproject's declared 3.0.0; what is unambiguously true is that the repo carries two mutually inconsistent version identities and this literal tracks neither by construction.

findings.title: model_resolver.py's 'WARNING:' stderr prefix diverges from the package's '<module>: ' convention
findings.description: `_load_profiles` prints `"WARNING: PyYAML not installed; using hardcoded model profiles"` (line 19), `"WARNING: cannot read model profiles %s: %s; using hardcoded fallback"` (lines 26-27), and `"WARNING: model profiles %s contains invalid YAML: %s; using hardcoded fallback"` (lines 30-31). Every sibling module that emits similar tolerant-fallback stderr diagnostics prefixes with its own lowercase module name instead: citations.py's `"citations: ..."`, ingest_tools.py's `"ingest: ..."`, dispatch.py's `"dispatch: ..."`, evidence.py's `"evidence: ..."`, synthesize.py's `"synthesize: ..."`.
findings.impact: A generic ALL-CAPS 'WARNING:' tag can't be grepped back to model_resolver.py specifically the way the rest of the package's messages can be traced to their source module, and it stands out as the one file using a different diagnostic convention.
findings.remediation: Prefix these three messages with `"model_resolver: "` to match the package-wide convention.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The core factual assertions check out. model_resolver.py lines 19, 26 and 30 emit the three quoted 'WARNING: ...' stderr messages verbatim, and a repo-wide grep for `WARNING|WARN:` across /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill shows model_resolver.py is the only file in the package using the ALL-CAPS 'WARNING:' tag (the nearest neighbour is synthesize.py:981 `print("WARN: %s" % w, ...)`, a different token). Every sibling prefix the claim names exists as described: citations.py:45 'citations: CWE catalog unavailable (%s); continuing without it'; ingest_tools.py:94 'ingest: excluded %d finding(s)...' (plus 'ingest skip/note/error' at 60, 66, 76, 81); dispatch.py:373/378/386/391/402/405/420/428/434 all 'dispatch: ...'; evidence.py:190/195/214/218 all 'evidence: ...'; synthesize.py:127/631/635/920/922/933/966 all 'synthesize: ...'. findings.title: Shell injection via unescaped fixture paths
findings.description: Fixture paths from the manifest are directly interpolated into a shell script string without escaping. An attacker-controlled manifest with paths containing shell metacharacters (quotes, semicolons, backticks) can break out of the intended if-statement context and execute arbitrary shell commands when the script is executed via `sh -c`.
findings.impact: An attacker who can modify the manifest.json file can execute arbitrary commands inside the Docker container, potentially compromising the build environment or exfiltrating data.
findings.remediation: Use shlex.quote() to escape each path before interpolating it into the shell script, or refactor to avoid shell script construction entirely by using subprocess with a list of arguments for each path check.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The mechanism is real and the cited lines are accurate. skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:49 collects `paths = [f["path"] for f in fixtures if f.get("path")]` straight out of the parsed manifest with zero validation (load_manifest at lines 91-99 does only json.loads; there is no schema check anywhere), and lines 53-56 interpolate each path into a shell program via f-string: `f'if [ -d "{p}" ]; then echo "PRESENT:{p}"; else echo "MISSING:{p}"; fi'`. The result is appended as the argument to `sh -c` at lines 52/57. Because the interpolation lands inside double quotes, a path containing a double quote, backtick, or `$(...)` escapes the test expression and executes arbitrary commands. I confirmed there is no escaping anywhere in the repo: a repo-wide grep for `shlex` and `shell=True` across all .py files returned no matches. So the code-level claim (CWE-78, unescaped interpolation into a shell string) is factually correct.

Two scoping corrections that argue against HIGH severity, which the auditor should weigh:
(1) Trust boundary. MANIFEST is hardcoded at line 13 to REPO_ROOT/tests/fixtures/manifest.json with no CLI or env override; grep for `manifest.json|MANIFEST` across all .py files shows this script is the sole reader. The only 'attacker-controlled manifest' scenario is an attacker who already has write access to the source tree — the same access needed to edit run_fixture_tests.py itself. No privilege boundary is crossed. The current manifest holds four benign literal paths under /opt/panopticon-fixtures.
(2) Blast radius. `subprocess.run(cmd, ...)` at line 58 is passed a list with no shell=True, so the host shell is never involved; the injected commands run only inside the `docker run --rm` container. Unlike run_tests() (lines 79-86), check_fixtures' docker invocation mounts no volumes and passes no host paths, so the injected code sees only the ephemeral image contents (public cloned goat apps and toolchains, per Dockerfile.fixtures) — no host filesystem, no secrets. Network egress is available by default, so image-content exfiltration is the realistic ceiling.
(3) Reachability. .github/workflows/ci.yml runs only ruff and `pytest tests/ -q`; grep of .github for `fixture` found no invocation of this script. It is a developer-local helper (DEVELOPMENT.md:79-80), not a CI-executed path, so the 'malicious PR touching only a data file' amplifier does not apply here.

Recommendation: keep the finding, apply the shlex.quote() remediation as defense-in-depth/hardening, but downgrade severity to LOW. Also note this is a verbatim duplicate of SI-001 in the same batch (same file, same lines, same mechanism) and should be deduplicated.

findings.title: Shell command injection via unescaped path interpolation
findings.description: Fixture paths from the manifest are directly interpolated into a shell script string without escaping. An attacker-controlled manifest with paths containing shell metacharacters (quotes, semicolons, backticks) can break out of the intended if-statement context and execute arbitrary shell commands when the script is executed via `sh -c`.
findings.impact: An attacker who can modify tests/fixtures/manifest.json can execute arbitrary shell commands in the Docker container environment during fixture tests.
findings.remediation: Use proper shell escaping or argument passing: use subprocess.run() with a list of arguments instead of sh -c, or use shlex.quote() to escape path values before interpolation.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Verified directly against the source, independent of any other claim. skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py lines 52-58 build a shell program by string interpolation and hand it to `sh -c`: line 52 `cmd = ["docker", "run", "--rm", tag, "sh", "-c"]`, lines 53-56 join per-path f-strings `f'if [ -d "{p}" ]; then echo "PRESENT:{p}"; else echo "MISSING:{p}"; fi'`, line 57 appends the joined script, line 58 executes it. The `p` values originate at line 49 from the manifest parsed at lines 91-99, which applies no validation or escaping. A path value containing `"`, a backtick, or `$(...)` breaks out of the quoted test and runs arbitrary commands. Repo-wide grep for `shlex` and `shell=True` in .py files returns zero matches, confirming no escaping exists anywhere. CWE-78 is the correct weakness class.

Same scoping caveats I established from the code: the manifest path is hardcoded (line 13) to an in-repo file that only this script reads, so exploitation presupposes source-tree write access equivalent to editing the script itself; `subprocess.run` at line 58 receives a list and no shell=True, so nothing reaches the host shell; and the check_fixtures docker invocation passes no `-v` mounts (contrast run_tests at lines 79-86, which does mount the repo read-only), confining execution to a throwaway container holding only public fixture clones and toolchains. .github/workflows/ci.yml does not invoke this script, and no workflow references it — it is a local dev helper per DEVELOPMENT.md:79-80.

Two metadata defects worth flagging: the category/lens is `known_vulns`, but this is an injection defect with no associated CVE — it belongs under `injection`; and the finding is a verbatim duplicate of INJCT-001 (identical file, overlapping line range, identical description text), so one of the pair should be dropped in dedup. findings.title: Unescaped f-string interpolation of fixture paths into sh -c in check_fixtures()
findings.description: `check_fixtures()` builds a POSIX shell script by directly interpolating each fixture's `path` value (sourced from tests/fixtures/manifest.json) into a double-quoted `[ -d "{p}" ]` test with an f-string (line 54), joins them with `;`, and passes the resulting string to `docker run --rm <tag> sh -c <script>` with no shlex.quote/escaping. Any path value containing a shell metacharacter (quote, backtick, $(), ;) breaks out of the quoted context and executes as a shell command inside the fixtures container.
findings.impact: Under current usage the paths originate from the repo-local, version-controlled manifest.json, so exploitation requires an attacker able to modify that file (e.g. a malicious PR), and this docker invocation is --rm with no volume mounts, limiting blast radius to the throwaway panopticon-fixtures image. It remains a live CWE-78 injection primitive that becomes exploitable the moment manifest.json's provenance is less trusted or this pattern is reused with externally influenced paths.
findings.remediation: Avoid building a shell string: check each path with a separate no-shell `docker run --rm tag test -d "<path>"` invocation, or at minimum wrap each interpolated path in shlex.quote() before joining into the sh -c script.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The code matches the description exactly. skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:49 collects `paths = [f["path"] for f in fixtures if f.get("path")]`, line 52 builds `cmd = ["docker", "run", "--rm", tag, "sh", "-c"]`, and lines 53-56 join per-path f-strings `f'if [ -d "{p}" ]; then echo "PRESENT:{p}"; else echo "MISSING:{p}"; fi'` with '; ' before appending as the sh -c argument at line 57 and executing at line 58. There is no shlex.quote and no import of shlex anywhere in the file; a path containing `"`, `` ` ``, `$(...)` or `;` escapes the double-quoted test and is evaluated by the container shell — a textbook CWE-78 sink. The claim's own scoping is also accurate and I verified it: the only call site is main() at line 125, feeding `manifest.get("fixtures", [])` from the fixed constant MANIFEST = REPO_ROOT/tests/fixtures/manifest.json (line 13); there is no CLI flag or env override for the manifest path, so today's inputs are the four repo-controlled, benign paths in tests/fixtures/manifest.json (all `/opt/panopticon-fixtures/<name>`). The docker invocation at line 52 has no -v mounts and uses --rm, so post-exploit impact is confined to the throwaway panopticon-fixtures container. Hence: real, present injection primitive gated behind write access to a version-controlled file — LOW severity and POSSIBLE exploitability are the right calibration, and the remediation (separate `docker run --rm tag test -d <path>` invocations, or shlex.quote) is sound.

findings.title: Self-asserted _group field can misattribute a finding to the wrong review group when the source filename doesn't match GROUP_RE
findings.description: `load_findings()` derives a finding's internal `_group` tag from the source filename via `GROUP_RE` (lines 119-120) and only overwrites `nf["_group"]` when that match succeeds. `normalize_finding()` mutates the finding dict in place and returns the same object, so if the incoming agent JSON already carries a `_group` key — an internal-only field never documented in the panel-review/lens-sweep finding schema — and the filename fails to match GROUP_RE (e.g. an unusual group name, or any file not produced through the standard dispatch out_file convention), the self-asserted value passes through untouched into build_report()'s per-group bucketing (lines 636-653), which decides which group's panel_grades/key_findings the finding is counted under, before being stripped from the final report at line 657.
findings.impact: A compromised or prompt-injected reviewer for one group could relabel one of its own findings into a different group's bucket, hiding it from the correct group's per-group grade/key_findings while it surfaces under an unrelated group. Global summary.stats/gate are unaffected, so this is a per-group reporting-integrity gap rather than a gate bypass, but can still mislead any consumer that gates or triages by per-group grade.
findings.remediation: Strip any pre-existing _group key from agent-authored JSON in load_findings() (fold it into the same denylist as SEC-201) before assigning the filename-derived value, rather than only conditionally overwriting it.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The mechanism described is exactly what the code does. In /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/synthesize.py, load_findings() strips only AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS = ('source', 'reinforced') (lines 93, 125-129), then computes `m = GROUP_RE.match(os.path.basename(path)); group = m.group(1) if m else None` (119-120) and assigns `nf['_group'] = group` ONLY `if group is not None` (131-132). normalize_finding() mutates and returns the same dict (line 85), so an agent-supplied `_group` key survives untouched whenever the filename does not match GROUP_RE. That value then drives per-group bucketing in build_report(): `gfind = [f for f in active if (f.get('_group') == g['name']) or (f.get('_group') not in known_groups and location.file in gfiles)]`, which feeds panel_grades and key_findings, and `_group` is only popped afterward. NOTE: the claim's line numbers for that block are off — the bucketing is at lines 654-671 and the strip is at line 675, not 636-653/657; load_findings' cited 119-133 is exact. The behaviour that a self-asserted `_group` fully controls group attribution is directly demonstrated by tests/test_synthesize.py:600-614 (TestGroupTag.test_test_panel_grade_reflects_test_findings), which passes a hand-written `_group: 'g1'` into build_report and asserts the group's test grade flips from A to D. Reachability of the precondition (filename not matching GROUP_RE): GROUP_RE = ^findings-(.+)-(code|test|security|architecture|database|redteam)(-panel_review|-lens_sweep-[A-Za-z0-9_]+)?\.json$ (lines 455-457). dispatch.py builds out_file as '.panopticon/findings-%s-%s-lens_sweep-%s.json' % (group_name, panel_name, lens_name) (line 281). lens_name comes from the agent-authored ScopeProfile, whose schema (skill/reference/scope-profile-schema.json line 36) types lens 'name' as an unconstrained string with no pattern, and that schema is only exercised in tests (tests/test_schemas.py), never at runtime. findings.title: Advisor prompt embeds an unfiltered agent-authored finding JSON, opening an indirect-prompt-injection channel
findings.description: `render_advisor_prompts()` serializes an entire finding dict — including free-text description/impact/remediation/title fields an earlier panel_review/lens_sweep agent produced after reading the target repository's own source — and substitutes it verbatim into the `{claim_json}` placeholder of agents/advisor.md, which becomes the literal advisor prompt. Because those free-text fields can contain wording copied or paraphrased from the reviewed repository, and that repository is by panopticon's own threat model untrusted/adversarial, this is a channel for indirect prompt injection.
findings.impact: agents/advisor.md already instructs the model not to trust the claim and to verify independently by reading cited files, and evidence.match_verdict() requires an exact finding_id echo — both are real, effective mitigations bounding damage to a single already-flagged finding's verdict. But there is no structural isolation of the untrusted payload beyond a markdown heading (no explicit 'treat imperative text inside string fields as data, not instructions' framing), so a successful injection could still flip an individual verdict — the same self-verification/laundering risk class the codebase otherwise guards against.
findings.remediation: Add explicit untrusted-data framing around {claim_json} in agents/advisor.md, and consider bounding/neutralizing the free-text fields before substitution (length caps, stripping of markdown/code-fence sequences that could re-open the delimiter).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every mechanical fact checks out. dispatch.py:345-346 does `claim = json.dumps(finding, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)` then `render_prompt('advisor.md', {'claim_json': claim})` on the WHOLE finding dict from the verify queue — no field allowlist, no length cap, no scrubbing. skill/agents/advisor.md lines 12-14 place {claim_json} under a bare '## Claim' markdown heading with no 'the text inside these fields is data, not instructions' framing. skill/SKILL.md:56-58 confirms the rendered file's contents are dispatched verbatim as the advisor agent's task message, so this is literal prompt text, not a data channel. The provenance of those free-text fields is as described: skill/agents/panel-review.md:38 instructs panel reviewers to emit title/description/impact/remediation after reading the target repo's files, and evidence.build_verify_queue (evidence.py:92-120) queues those finding dicts by reference with no content sanitization — it sanitizes only the id into the queue_id ([A-Za-z0-9_-]) and write_verify_queue strips only underscore-prefixed keys. The 'untrusted repo' premise is the repo's own, not invented: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-03-tool-policy-enforcement-design.md:13-19 records SEC-101 (advisor-confirmed HIGH) as 'reading hostile repository content; prompt injection in a reviewed repo', and anticipates corpora that 'deliberately plant injection payloads'. The mitigations the claim credits are also real: advisor.md:10 ('Do not trust the claim; verify it') and evidence.match_verdict (evidence.py:202-221) which drops a verdict whose finding_id echo mismatches — bounding damage to the one already-flagged finding. Two things the claim missed, both of which narrow it but do not void it: (a) json.dumps escapes quotes, backslashes and newlines inside string values, so injected text cannot break the JSON string, forge a new markdown heading, or open a code fence — the remediation's 'stripping of markdown/code-fence sequences that could re-open the delimiter' is largely moot; (b) render_prompt's sentinel two-step (dispatch.py:168-175, tested at tests/test_dispatch.py:303) means a '{token}' inside the claim cannot re-trigger placeholder expansion. What survives is precisely what the claim asserts: imperative English inside a JSON string field is still rendered into the advisor's instruction stream with no data/instruction boundary. I mark LIKELY rather than CERTAIN because whether such wording actually flips a verdict is a model-behavior question the repository cannot settle — which matches the claim's own POSSIBLE/LOW scoping. One downstream amplifier worth flagging to the auditor: evidence.apply_verdict (evidence.py:235) copies the advisor's `reasoning` into provenance.confirmation_reasoning, which then flows into the synthesized report and HTML, so a manipulated verdict's prose propagates beyond the single verdict decision. On citations: CWE-94 (code injection) is a poor fit and I would not carry it; CWE-1427 (Improper Neutralization of Input Used for LLM Prompting) and OWASP LLM01 Prompt Injection are the correct anchors, and A03:2021 is not.

findings.title: Self-contained HTML report ships an inline <script> with no Content-Security-Policy
findings.description: `_html_doc()` emits a <style> block and an inline <script>{_JS}</script> but no Content-Security-Policy meta tag. Every dynamic field reaching the document today is correctly passed through _escape() (html.escape, quote=True) before interpolation (verified across _render_card, _render_provenance, _render_heatmap, etc.), so there is no live XSS, but the document has no defense-in-depth against a future regression, and the report renders agent- and tool-authored strings that ultimately reflect content from the potentially adversarial reviewed repository.
findings.impact: Low today — no injection point exists — but a future escaping regression in the finding-rendering helpers would fail open (execute) rather than fail closed, and if the report is ever hosted over HTTP without an external CSP header this is the only layer available.
findings.remediation: Add a restrictive CSP meta tag in _html_doc(), or better, hash/nonce the inline _JS/_CSS blocks and drop 'unsafe-inline' for script-src so an escaping regression is contained.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. `_html_doc()` at /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/html_report.py:177-193 emits `<meta charset>`, `<meta name=viewport>`, `<title>`, `<style>{_CSS}</style>` and `<script>{_JS}</script>` and no `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">`. A repo-wide grep for 'Content-Security-Policy|csp' (case-insensitive) returns only doc/report artifacts and unrelated '.csproj' hits — no CSP is emitted anywhere, and there is no wrapper that injects one (write_html/render at lines 676-702 pass straight through to _html_doc). The claim's supporting facts also hold: `_escape` (line 172-174) is `html.escape(str(value))`, whose default is quote=True, and I traced every dynamic interpolation in _render_header, _render_card, _render_provenance, _render_heatmap, _render_bar_chart, _render_dashboard, _render_compare_* and found no unescaped sink — the only raw interpolations are module constants (_SEV_ORDER/_PANEL_ORDER tokens, formatted floats/ints) or values sanitized by _severity_class/_panel_class/the re.sub at line 315. So the claim's own 'no live XSS today' qualifier is accurate. The untrusted-data premise is also real: finding titles and location.file flow from SARIF tool output (sarif_utils.sarif_to_findings lines 95-108) which echoes matched content and paths from the reviewed repository. This is correctly filed as INFO/defense-in-depth, not a live vulnerability. One caveat for the remediation: because _CSS is inline and _render_bar_chart emits inline `style='width: ...'` attributes (line 425), a CSP would need style-src 'unsafe-inline' or hashes/nonces, so only script-src can be tightened without further refactoring.

findings.title: Untested fixture test orchestration logic
findings.description: run_fixture_tests.py has no unit tests. The main() function (lines 102-138) orchestrates Docker image building, fixture validation, and pytest execution. Complex conditional logic (lines 119-132) handles image existence, rebuild requirements, and fixture presence checks with no test coverage.
findings.impact: Docker integration issues, fixture validation failures, and test execution problems may not be detected until CI runtime, increasing time-to-feedback.
findings.remediation: Add unit tests (with mocked Docker calls) covering image existence checks, build_image() invocation, check_fixtures() with present/missing fixtures, and run_tests() with various exit codes.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The factual core — run_fixture_tests.py has no unit tests — is verified. Grep for `run_fixture_tests|check_fixtures` under tests/ returns no files. A broader grep for `run_fixture_tests|check_fixtures|build_image|docker_available` across all .py files shows the only test-side hits are in tests/test_run_tools.py, and those exercise `rt.docker_available` from skill/scripts/run_tools.py:36 — a different module with a completely different signature (`docker_available(image="panopticon-tools", runner=None)`). run_fixture_tests.py defines its own zero-arg `docker_available()` at line 22 that is never imported by any test. I enumerated tests/**/*.py (38 files) and none targets this module. main() does span lines 102-138 as claimed, with the branch logic at 119-132 as described, and the module has no `__init__`-style seam for injection.

A structural point that supports the remediation: unlike run_tools.docker_available, which accepts a `runner=` callable precisely so tests can inject a fake (see tests/test_run_tools.py:12-24), every function in run_fixture_tests.py calls subprocess.run directly with no injection point. Any unit test would have to monkeypatch the module's `subprocess` attribute, or the module would need the same `runner=` seam its sibling already uses — that sibling is the natural template.

Two corrections for the auditor. (1) Severity HIGH is not supportable. This module is a developer-local convenience wrapper (DEVELOPMENT.md:74-83) that is not executed by CI — .github/workflows/ci.yml runs only ruff plus `pytest tests/ -q`, and no workflow references it. It contains no product logic and ships no runtime behavior to users; a regression here breaks a local dev command, not the scanner or the CI gate. The stated impact ('may not be detected until CI runtime') is itself inaccurate, since this code never runs in CI. LOW is the defensible severity. (2) The CWE-391 citation is wrong and already marked verified:false — CWE-391 is 'Unchecked Error Condition', which has no relationship to missing unit-test coverage. It should be dropped rather than carried as an unverified citation.

findings.title: Citation enrichment exception handling not directly tested
findings.description: The enrich_citations() function (lines 219-280) contains a broad exception handler at line 266 that catches all exceptions during citation enrichment. This is intentionally tolerant to prevent synthesis failures, but the exception path (lines 266-269) lacks explicit test coverage for the graceful degradation behavior when enrichment fails.
findings.impact: Silent failures in citation enrichment could result in findings without CWE/OWASP mappings. Debugging citation issues becomes difficult without test validation of error handling.
findings.remediation: Add test cases in test_citations.py for enrich_citations() covering malformed citation data causing exception, that findings still serialize correctly, and that citation_quality is set to 'none' on error.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The cited code exists as described: enrich_citations spans skill/scripts/citations.py:219-280, and lines 266-269 are a catch-all `except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001` that prints 'citation enrich error (finding %s): %s' to stderr, pops 'citations', and sets f['citation_quality'] = 'none'. I read every enrich_citations call site in the test tree (tests/test_citations.py lines 29, 183, 188, 193, 199, 206, 211, 219, 228, 237, 250, 259, 264, 269, 279, 290, 303, 315) and traced the inputs through the try block. None of them can reach the handler: the closest candidate, test_enrich_tolerant_of_malformed_subfields (lines 308-318), passes citations={'ssvc': 'active'}, {'cwe': 89}, {'cve': 5, 'owasp': 1}, all of which are absorbed by the isinstance guards at lines 208, 244-245, 250 before any exception can be raised — that test exercises the tolerant *happy* path, not the except path. No test anywhere asserts the 'citation enrich error' stderr string (grep across all .py files returns only citations.py:267). So the graceful-degradation branch has zero direct coverage, exactly as claimed. The path is also genuinely reachable and therefore testable: validate_cwe does an unguarded `catalog['cwe']` (line 60), so a caller passing a catalog dict not produced by load_cwe_catalog raises KeyError inside the try. Two caveats on the claim's framing that do not change the verdict: (a) the failure is not 'silent' — it logs to stderr with the finding id; (b) production callers (synthesize.py:638 and 942) always pass a catalog built by citations.load_cwe_catalog(), which guarantees the 'cwe'/'cwe_owasp'/'owasp_top10' keys, so in-tree the branch is defensive rather than routinely hit. That makes MEDIUM arguably generous for a pure coverage gap, but the factual assertion — lines 266-269 lack explicit test coverage — is verified. Note the attached citation CWE-391 (Unchecked Error Condition) is a poor fit: the error is checked, caught, and logged; the issue is untested error handling, not an unchecked condition.

findings.title: Git operation error handling in collect_changed_files() lacks test coverage

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Verified the code and the whole test suite. parse_template_frontmatter (skill/scripts/dispatch.py:21-67) has five ValueError raise sites: line 36 (no frontmatter block), 39 (unterminated block), 54 (unparseable line), 63 (missing name/description), 66 (tool_policy missing allowed/forbidden). name: a
---
body' hits line 63 — note the inline comment on line 47 says '# missing tool_policy', but the required-scalar loop at 61-63 runs BEFORE the tool_policy loop at 64-66, so that case raises on the missing 'description' and line 66 is never reached. findings.title: test_synthesize.py calls unittest.mock.patch without importing unittest.mock
findings.description: tests/test_synthesize.py only does `import unittest` at line 7 - there is no `import unittest.mock` or `from unittest import mock` anywhere in the file. Yet TestHtmlOut.test_compare_missing_file_errors_cleanly (line 1027) and test_compare_invalid_json_errors_cleanly (line 1050) both reference `unittest.mock.patch("sys.stderr", ...)`. `unittest.mock` is a separate submodule that Python does not auto-attach to the `unittest` package on a bare `import unittest`; the `.mock` attribute only exists on the `unittest` module object once something in the process has explicitly imported `unittest.mock`. Sibling test files that use mocking (tests/test_dispatch.py:8, tests/test_model_resolver.py:7, and the files under tests/tools/) all do `from unittest import mock` / `from unittest.mock import patch` explicitly - this file is the outlier.
findings.impact: The two tests pass today only as a side effect of pytest's whole-directory collection order: some sibling module (alphabetically collected before this one, e.g. tests/test_model_resolver.py) imports unittest.mock first and binds it onto the shared unittest module object in sys.modules, which every other module in the same process then sees. Run this file in isolation - e.g. `pytest tests/test_synthesize.py::TestHtmlOut -v`, which is literally the invocation documented in docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-html-report.md - and both tests raise `AttributeError: module 'unittest' has no attribute 'mock'` instead of exercising the intended stderr-capture/error-path assertions. There is no conftest.py or tests/__init__.py in the repo to pre-import it either.
findings.remediation: Add `from unittest import mock` to the top-level imports of tests/test_synthesize.py and reference it as `mock.patch(...)` at both call sites, matching the pattern already used in tests/test_dispatch.py and tests/test_model_resolver.py.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_synthesize.py imports only `import unittest` (line 7); its module-level imports are contextlib, io, os, sys, json, tempfile, unittest, plus `import scripts.synthesize as syn` (line 10) and a late `import scripts.evidence as evidence_mod` (line 1482). A grep of the whole file for `mock` shows exactly two hits, both uses and no import: line 1027 in TestHtmlOut.test_compare_missing_file_errors_cleanly and line 1050 in test_compare_invalid_json_errors_cleanly, each `with unittest.mock.patch("sys.stderr", new_callable=io.StringIO) as captured:`. Both are on the straight-line body of the test (no skip/guard), so they execute on every run. A repo-wide grep for `unittest.mock|from unittest import mock|from unittest.mock import` shows the only other sources are sibling test files (tests/test_dispatch.py:8, tests/test_model_resolver.py:7, tests/tools/test_base.py:5 and seven other tests/tools files) and docs; nothing under skill/scripts/ imports it, so the transitive import chain of `scripts.synthesize` (citations, evidence, html_report, ingest_tools -- all stdlib-only per the module docstring) does not bring `unittest.mock` in either. There is no conftest.py anywhere in the repo (Glob **/conftest.py returned nothing) and no tests/__init__.py, so nothing pre-imports it at collection setup. CPython's unittest/__init__.py imports .result/.case/.suite/.loader/.main/.runner/.signals and provides only IsolatedAsyncioTestCase lazily via module __getattr__; `mock` is not among them, so `import unittest` alone does not bind `unittest.mock`. The whole-suite invocation documented in CONTRIBUTING.md:13 and .github/workflows/ci.yml:41 (`python -m pytest tests/ -q`) collects test_dispatch.py and test_model_resolver.py before test_synthesize.py alphabetically, which is why it passes today. The isolated invocation the claim cites is real: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-html-report.md lines 927 and 997 both say `Run: pytest tests/test_synthesize.py::TestHtmlOut -v`. CI installs bare `pytest ruff pyyaml jsonschema` (ci.yml:39) with no pytest-mock, and pytest deliberately probes `sys.modules.get("unittest.mock")` rather than importing it, so in that isolated run the attribute lookup would raise AttributeError before the assertions run. Residual caveat (does not change the verdict): I cannot execute code, so I cannot rule out that some plugin in an individual developer's site-packages happens to pre-import unittest.mock -- but that is exactly the accidental, undeclared dependency the claim describes. Ruff's configured rule set in pyproject.toml (E, F, W) does not flag submodule attribute access, so linting will not catch it. Severity MEDIUM is defensible for a latent test-integrity defect; note the failure mode is a loud AttributeError, not a silently-passing test.

findings.title: run_fixture_tests.py has no unit tests and no injectable subprocess seam
findings.description: There is no tests/test_run_fixture_tests.py anywhere in the repo, so `load_manifest`, `check_fixtures`, `image_exists`, `docker_available`, `build_image`, `run_tests`, and `main`'s argument handling have zero automated test coverage. This is unlike the closely related skill/scripts/run_tools.py, which was explicitly refactored to accept an injectable `runner` parameter precisely so its docker-invoking logic could be unit tested with fakes (see tests/test_run_tools.py). run_fixture_tests.py instead calls `subprocess.run` directly and unconditionally in docker_available, image_exists, build_image, and run_tests (lines 17-19, 23-27, 31-35, 38-44, 79-88), with no parameter to substitute a fake process.
findings.impact: Pure, easily-testable logic — manifest JSON parsing/validation, the PRESENT:/MISSING: stdout-parsing in check_fixtures, and the pytest-args construction in run_tests — can regress silently, since the only way this code is exercised is by actually building the panopticon-fixtures Docker image, a manual/CI-gated integration path not part of `pytest tests/ -q`.
findings.remediation: Add tests/test_run_fixture_tests.py covering load_manifest and check_fixtures's stdout-parsing, and give docker_available/image_exists/build_image/run_tests an injectable runner parameter mirroring run_tools.py's pattern.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified. Glob of tests/**/*.py returns 39 test files and none is test_run_fixture_tests.py; a grep for `run_fixture_tests|check_fixtures|load_manifest|image_exists|docker_available|build_image` restricted to tests/ matches only tests/test_run_tools.py lines 12/14/17/24, which exercise run_tools.docker_available, not the fixture script. A repo-wide grep confirms `check_fixtures` appears in exactly two places, both inside skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py (definition line 47, call site line 125). The seam contrast is real: skill/scripts/run_tools.py:36-44 defines `def docker_available(image="panopticon-tools", runner=None)` with `runner = runner or subprocess.run`, and tests/test_run_tools.py injects fakes for both docker_available and run_tools. By contrast run_fixture_tests.py hardcodes subprocess: `run()` at line 19, docker_available at 23-26, image_exists at 31-34, check_fixtures at 58, run_tests at 87 — none accept a runner. The untestable-in-CI claim also holds: .github/workflows/ci.yml:41 runs only `python -m pytest tests/ -q`, and nothing in .github invokes run_fixture_tests.py (it is documented as a manual command at DEVELOPMENT.md:79-80). findings.title: citations.normalize_cwe_entries is unused in production code and untested
findings.description: `normalize_cwe_entries` (citations.py:66-80) is exported from the module but is not called anywhere in citations.py's own pipeline — `enrich_citations` builds its CWE list via `_raw_cwe_ids` + `validate_cwe` directly (lines 232-235) rather than through this helper — nor is it called from any other file under skill/. Grepping the whole test tree turns up zero references to the function.
findings.impact: This is either genuinely dead code (unnecessary maintenance surface) or a helper that some caller was meant to use and doesn't (a latent integration gap). Either way it sits with no regression protection: the documented behavior could silently break and nothing would notice.
findings.remediation: Either delete normalize_cwe_entries if confirmed unused, or wire it into its intended call site and add unit tests for its three documented behaviors.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified independently on all three points. (1) The function exists exactly at skill/scripts/citations.py:66-80 with the three documented behaviors (dicts preserved as-is, strings validated via validate_cwe, invalid entries dropped). (2) A repo-wide grep for `normalize_cwe_entries` returns exactly two kinds of hit: the definition at citations.py:66, and text inside docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-self-scan-report.json (which is this same finding already serialized into a prior scan report, not a call site). There are zero call sites in skill/, tests/, or anywhere else. A separate grep scoped to skill/ for `normalize_cwe|citations\.[a-z_]+` confirms the only citations-module entry points used in production are load_cwe_catalog and enrich_citations (synthesize.py:941-942 and :638); the similarly named `_normalize_cwe` at skill/scripts/tools/dependency_check.py:45 is an unrelated private method on a different class. (3) The claim's account of the bypass is accurate: enrich_citations builds its CWE list inline at citations.py:232-235 via `for cid in _raw_cwe_ids(raw): v = validate_cwe(cid, catalog, tool_sourced=tool_sourced)`, which duplicates normalize_cwe_entries' logic with one meaningful behavioral difference — _raw_cwe_ids (lines 205-216) unwraps dict entries to their 'id' and re-validates them, whereas normalize_cwe_entries passes dicts through unvalidated. So the helper is not merely redundant, it would produce different (weaker) output than the inline path if wired in, which strengthens 'delete it' over 'wire it in'. (4) tests/test_citations.py contains no reference to it: the module's other public functions all have dedicated tests (validate_cwe at lines 36-65, derive_owasp at 55-59, ssvc_decide at 77-101, epss_lookup at 117-168, enrich_citations throughout), making this the sole untested public export. CWE-561 (Dead Code) is an apt citation. Severity LOW is appropriate — this is maintenance surface, not a defect.
