Every assertion is a bare `assertIn` substring check against the raw text of skill/prompts/lenses.md, skill/agents/scout.md, and skill/reference/security-checklists.md. Nothing checks structure, ordering, section headings, or that the strings appear in a meaningful position (e.g. 'structure' would satisfy test_lenses_cover_all_nine if it appeared anywhere in the file, including inside an unrelated sentence). So 'minimal asset validation coverage' is an accurate description of this file.

Three caveats materially weaken the claim's stated impact and its remediation list, and are why confidence is POSSIBLE rather than CERTAIN:
(1) 'missing asset files' is already covered: `_read()` (lines 8-10) calls `open()` with no exception handling, so a deleted or renamed asset makes all three tests error out loudly. A dedicated test for that case would be redundant.
(2) 'surface/language combinations' are partly covered already — the tests enumerate four surfaces (db_sql, http_web, auth, crypto) and five languages (Ruby, Python, JavaScript, Java, Go).
(3) The impact sentence 'Broken or malformed asset files may not be detected until runtime' overstates the exposure for these three specific assets. None of them is parsed by any Python code: grepping the repo, skill/prompts/lenses.md is referenced only by DEVELOPMENT.md line 43 and this test; skill/reference/security-checklists.md is referenced only as prose inside skill/agents/panel-review.md line 25 (an agent reads it with the Read tool at runtime — there is no parser to break). skill/agents/scout.md, by contrast, is heavily covered elsewhere: tests/test_agent_templates.py exercises frontmatter parsing, missing-template and malformed-frontmatter fail-fast paths, and tests/test_dispatch.py's TestRenderGoldens does a byte-for-byte comparison of the rendered scout.md/panel-review.md/lens-sweep.md against tests/goldens/*.rendered.txt. The lens_sweep reviewer that filed this claim appears not to have accounted for that complementary coverage.

Net: the description is true as written and the gap is real but narrow and LOW-value; the enumerated remediation items are partly already satisfied. The cited CWE-1164 ('Irrelevant Code') does not fit a coverage gap and I do not endorse it.

findings.title: Missing citation_quality coverage through verdict paths
findings.description: test_missing_citation_quality_defaults_none (lines 87-90) tests the default when citation_quality is deleted, but no tests verify citation_quality propagation and transformation through different verdict types (CONFIRMED, REJECTED, NEEDS_MORE_INFO) and evidence status combinations.
findings.impact: Citation quality downgrades or upgrades during verdict processing may not be properly validated.
findings.remediation: Add tests for citation_quality changes across verdict types: verify that REJECTED status lowers quality, that tool_confirmed preserves quality, and that corroborated findings properly inherit quality.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The coverage gap is real and I verified it exhaustively. derive_evidence (/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/evidence.py:34-71) has five return branches, each independently carrying `"citation_quality": quality` (lines 49, 56, 63, 69, 71). Only two of those branches have a test asserting the value: the tool_confirmed branch (tests/test_evidence.py:26, asserts 'partial') and the unverified branch (tests/test_evidence.py:87-90, the cited default-to-'none' test). The advisor-verdict branch (evidence.py:57-63, serving CONFIRMED/REJECTED/NEEDS_MORE_INFO), the reinforced branch (50-56) and the corroborated branch (64-69) have no citation_quality assertion in any test — test_confirmed_verdict_is_advisor_confirmed, test_rejected_verdict_is_rejected, test_needs_more_info_verdict, test_verdict_beats_corroboration, test_tool_beats_verdict, test_cross_panel_corroborated and test_reinforced_is_tool_confirmed all assert only status/verified_by/reasoning. I grepped citation_quality across every .py file in the repo to check for coverage elsewhere: the only other assertion on a derived evidence.citation_quality is test_citation_quality_lives_in_evidence (/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_synthesize.py:1196-1201), and it (a) exercises only the unverified path (no verdicts passed) and (b) asserts merely `assertIn(..., ('full','partial','minimal','none'))`, which 'none' satisfies. So a regression that hardcoded the verdict branch to 'none' or dropped the key's value would pass the entire suite. tests/test_citations.py only covers _compute_citation_quality upstream of evidence derivation, and tests/test_html_report.py hand-constructs evidence dicts rather than deriving them, so neither closes the gap. Two caveats the auditor should carry forward: the claim's framing of 'transformation' and its remediation ('verify that REJECTED status lowers quality') describe behavior that does not exist — quality is read once at evidence.py:42 and passed through unchanged on every branch, so the correct test to add is a passthrough/invariance test, not a downgrade test. And the impact is narrower than MEDIUM suggests: citation_quality is consumed only for HTML rendering (skill/scripts/html_report.py:496-497) and is stripped from the finding body at synthesize.py:642; it does not feed grading or the gate (GATE_ELIGIBLE_DEFAULT keys on status only). The CWE-1164 citation is unverified and does not bear on the verdict.

findings.title: Magic number without explanation in test
findings.description: Line 39 uses range(37) to generate a list of test files: ['a/f%02d.py' % i for i in range(37)]. The significance of the number 37 is unexplained - there is no comment explaining why this specific value was chosen for testing.
findings.impact: Makes the test harder to maintain and understand. It's unclear if 37 is significant or arbitrary, or if it's meant to test a specific edge case.
findings.remediation: Add a comment explaining the choice: '# Test with 37 files to verify chunking with remainder: 37 % 15 = 7'

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The cited code exists exactly as described. tests/test_orchestrator.py line 39 (inside TestChunkFiles.test_never_exceeds_max_per, def at line 38) reads `files = ["a/f%02d.py" % i for i in range(37)]`, and there is no comment anywhere in the 37-42 block, nor a module- or class-level note, explaining the choice of 37. I read the entire file to rule out an explanatory comment elsewhere. The number is in fact load-bearing rather than arbitrary: chunk_files (skill/scripts/orchestrator.py:179-199) buckets by dirname, so all 37 files land in one directory bucket, are sliced into blocks of max_per=15, and produce chunks of [15, 15, 7] — 37 = 2*15 + 7 exercises the trailing-remainder path, which a multiple of 15 would not. So the claim's assertion that a reader cannot tell whether 37 is significant is fair, and the suggested remediation comment ('37 % 15 = 7') is arithmetically correct. Two qualifications that bound the severity: (a) the literal is partially self-documenting because line 42 asserts `sum(len(c) for c in chunks) == 37`, tying the input size to the assertion; (b) the same pattern appears unremarked elsewhere in the file (line 235, `range(5)` with max_per_group=2 asserting 3 groups), so this is a suite-wide stylistic habit rather than an isolated defect. This is a cosmetic maintainability nit with no correctness or behavioral impact; LOW (arguably INFO) is the right ceiling. The claim's CWE/citation fields are empty, which is appropriate — no security weakness is implicated.

findings.title: Undocumented test double lacks contract specification
findings.description: The _FakeResp class (lines 104-114) is a test double (fake object) that simulates an HTTP response object with context manager and file-like read() interface. It lacks documentation explaining what it simulates, what its contract is, or what callers should expect from its behavior.
findings.impact: Test code is harder to understand. Developers must read the implementation to understand what this fake is simulating and how it should be used.
findings.remediation: Add a docstring: '"""Simulates urllib.urlopen response object for testing EPSS lookup."""' and document the read() method's return value and behavior.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The factual assertion is exactly right and trivially checkable: tests/test_citations.py:104-114 defines `class _FakeResp` with `__init__`, `read(self, amt=None)`, `__enter__` and `__exit__`, and there is no class docstring and no method docstrings anywhere in it. It is indeed a test double for the urlopen response consumed by citations.epss_lookup (skill/scripts/citations.py:154-155, `with opener(req, timeout=8) as resp: payload = json.loads(resp.read(1000000))`), which is why it needs both the context-manager protocol and a size-capped `read`. Its `last_read_size` attribute exists specifically so test_request_capped_read_and_user_agent (tests/test_citations.py:157-168) can assert the 1000000-byte cap. So the class does carry an implicit contract that is not written down. That said, I want to be honest with the auditor about weight: this is an 11-line, single-file-local fake whose entire behaviour is visible in one screenful, used by five tests in the same file, and its non-obvious member (`last_read_size`) is named self-descriptively and asserted on directly. The stated impact ('developers must read the implementation') applies to essentially every inline test fake and does not distinguish this one. I confirm the finding as literally true but would treat it as noise-floor / non-actionable; LOW is the correct ceiling and dropping it entirely would be reasonable.

findings.title: test_clean_group_is_shallow exercises a panels input that build_result can never actually produce, masking that 'shallow' depth is dead in the real pipeline
findings.description: This test calls orchestrator._compute_depth(files, panels, security_mode) directly with a hand-picked panels=["code"] list that omits "security". But orchestrator.compute_group_panels (orchestrator.py, used by build_result for every real invocation) unconditionally appends "security" to panels whenever security_mode != "redteam" (the default). _compute_depth's logic is: return "deep" for redteam; return "standard" if any(p in ("security","redteam","database") for p in panels); otherwise return "shallow". Because "security" is always present in panels for the default/standard security_mode, the second branch always fires and the final `return "shallow"` line is unreachable through build_result/compute_group_panels -- i.e. through every real code path in the repo. The test only demonstrates the function's behavior in isolation with an input the production pipeline cannot generate; no test in test_orchestrator.py or test_dispatch_integration.py asserts that build_result(...) itself ever yields depth=="shallow" for a plain docs/style-only group.
findings.impact: The 'shallow' depth tier -- documented in tests/goldens/scout.rendered.txt as 'style/docs-only changes with no risky surfaces' and used by depth_planner.plan_lenses to cap lens-sweep spawning at 0-1 agents -- is effectively dead in the shipped orchestrator for the default (non-redteam) security mode. Every group produced by --repo-scan/--group/--directory/etc. in standard mode gets depth='standard' regardless of content, meaning trivial/docs-only changes are dispatched with the same lens-sweep budget as risky ones, inflating review cost. Because the only test asserting 'shallow' output calls the private helper directly with an unrealistic panels argument, this regression (which appears to already exist) is invisible to the test suite.
findings.remediation: Add an integration-level test that calls orchestrator.build_result(...) with security_mode='standard' and a docs/style-only file list, and asserts the resulting group depth is 'shallow'. If it is not (as analysis here suggests), fix compute_group_panels/_compute_depth so the security panel's unconditional inclusion doesn't collapse every group to 'standard' depth, then keep the unit test on _compute_depth as a supplementary (not sole) check.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified each factual link. (1) tests/test_orchestrator.py:333-335 calls the private helper directly: `orch._compute_depth(["docs/style.md"], ["code"], "standard")` and asserts 'shallow'. (2) skill/scripts/orchestrator.py:418-430 `_compute_depth` returns 'deep' for redteam, then 'standard' if any file is architecture/database/risky, then 'standard' if `any(p in ("security", "redteam", "database") for p in panels)`, else 'shallow'. (3) skill/scripts/orchestrator.py:99-116 `compute_group_panels` unconditionally appends 'redteam' when security_mode == 'redteam' and otherwise unconditionally appends 'security' — there is no branch in which the returned panels list lacks one of those two tokens. (4) skill/scripts/orchestrator.py:445-447 `build_result` computes `panels = compute_group_panels(c, security_mode)` and immediately `depth = _compute_depth(c, panels, security_mode)`, i.e. it can never pass a panels list without 'security'/'redteam'. Therefore for every group built by build_result: redteam -> 'deep', anything else -> 'standard'. The `return "shallow"` at orchestrator.py:430 is unreachable through build_result for ALL security_mode values (argparse restricts to standard|redteam, and even an arbitrary third value still takes the else-branch that appends 'security'). Grep confirms the only callers of `_compute_depth` in the repo are orchestrator.py:447 and the test at test_orchestrator.py:334. (5) The claim that no test asserts build_result itself yields 'shallow' also holds: tests/test_dispatch_integration.py:19-20 is the closest — it calls `orch.build_result(td, "repo", ".", None, ["docs/readme.md"], [], 15)` then reads `result["groups"][0].get("depth", "standard")` and only asserts `sweep_count <= 1` with a single-lens profile, which passes regardless of the depth value, so it cannot detect the collapse. Caveat on impact (does not change the verdict, but argues the severity is lower than MEDIUM): the runtime dispatch budget is driven by the SCOUT's ScopeProfile depth, not by groups.json — skill/scripts/dispatch.py:235 reads `scope_profile.get("depth", "standard")` and skill/scripts/depth_planner.py:22 likewise, while skill/SKILL.md:43-44 states only the group name, file list, and security_mode are appended to the scout prompt. So orchestrator's per-group `depth` field appears not to be consumed downstream at all, meaning the practical cost inflation the claim describes is speculative; what is verified is dead code (CWE-561) in `_compute_depth` plus a unit test whose passing input the production caller cannot generate.

findings.title: Category-derived CWE fallback is only tested for one of twelve categories, hiding that three overrides point to CWE ids missing from the shipped catalog
findings.description: citations.CATEGORY_CWE_OVERRIDES maps 12 category names to CWE ids for use by citations._derive_cwe_from_category when a finding has no explicit CWE. That helper only returns a citation `if cid and cid in catalog["cwe"]` (citations.py:177-181). Checking skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json's "cwe" map against the override table shows three of the twelve overrides reference CWE ids that are NOT present in the catalog: "config"->CWE-16, "logging"->CWE-778, "headers"->CWE-693. For findings in those three categories, _derive_cwe_from_category silently returns None and enrich_citations falls back to citation_quality="none" instead of the intended "minimal". test_citations.py's only test of this fallback path, test_category_mapping, exercises exclusively the "injection" category (CWE-89, which IS in the catalog), so the silent-failure branch for config/logging/headers has zero coverage.
findings.impact: Findings synthesized with category='config', 'logging', or 'headers' never receive a derived CWE citation and are scored citation_quality='none' rather than 'minimal', degrading their evidence/citation quality in the final report for no reason discoverable from the code's own declared intent (the override table explicitly lists a mapping for them). This mismatch between CATEGORY_CWE_OVERRIDES and the shipped catalog has existed undetected because no test exercises those three categories.
findings.remediation: Add test cases for category='config', 'logging', and 'headers' (parallel to test_category_mapping) that assert the current (broken) 'none' outcome, or fix the underlying issue by adding CWE-16, CWE-778, and CWE-693 to skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json's "cwe" map and updating the tests to assert the corrected 'minimal' outcome with the derived CWE present.
references: skill/scripts/citations.py:177-181 (_derive_cwe_from_category silently returns None when cid not in catalog)
tests/test_citations.py:209-215 and tests/test_citations.py:231-239 (both derivation tests use CWE-89 categories)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Both halves of the claim verify. Data mismatch: CATEGORY_CWE_OVERRIDES (skill/scripts/citations.py:16-29) maps exactly 12 categories; I read skill/reference/cwe-catalog.json in full (34 entries in the 'cwe' map) and grepped it for CWE-16, CWE-778 and CWE-693 — zero matches. The other nine override targets (CWE-89, 79, 287, 327, 352, 918, 22, 78, and 89 again for sql_injection) are all present. Behaviour: `_derive_cwe_from_category` (citations.py:177-181) gates on `if cid and cid in catalog['cwe']`, so for category 'config', 'logging' or 'headers' it returns None. In `enrich_citations` (citations.py:255-261) that leaves `clean` empty for a finding with no other citations, and `_compute_citation_quality({}, None)` (citations.py:184-186) hits `if not citations: return 'minimal' if finding_cvss else 'none'` — so the finding is scored 'none', not the 'minimal' the override table implies. I traced the resulting label: it is copied into evidence.citation_quality (evidence.py:42-71) and rendered in the HTML card (html_report.py:496-497); it does NOT feed gate_verdict (synthesize.py:430-441) or triage_priority (evidence.py:74-89), so the impact is report-metadata quality only, which is what the claim asserts. Coverage: grepping tests/ for the three category names finds only tests/test_html_report.py:459 ('config' used for top-category counting, not citation derivation); no test in tests/test_citations.py or tests/test_synthesize.py exercises the derivation path for config/logging/headers. One minor inaccuracy in the claim's wording: test_category_mapping is not the *only* test of the fallback path — test_category_derived_cwe_with_top_level_cvss_is_minimal (tests/test_citations.py:231-239) also exercises it with category 'sql_injection'. That does not change the conclusion, since sql_injection also maps to CWE-89, which is in the catalog; the three broken overrides remain at zero coverage. Given that the only consequence is a metadata label with no gate or triage effect, MEDIUM reads slightly high to me and LOW would be defensible, but the finding itself is factually correct and actionable.

findings.title: dispatch.main()'s --model-lens-sweep/--model-panel-review/--model-advisor and --agents-dir CLI flags are never exercised
findings.description: dispatch.py's main() parses --model-lens-sweep, --model-panel-review, --model-advisor (wired into the `overrides` dict passed to build_plan) and --agents-dir (passed through to build_plan's enforcement-detection logic). Every test in test_dispatch.py that touches model overrides or agents_dir calls dispatch.build_plan(...) directly with Python kwargs (e.g. agents_dir=d at lines 93, 245, 394, 402, 412); none of them invoke dispatch.main([...]) with these flags on the argv list, so the argparse wiring itself (turning --model-advisor foo into overrides["advisor"]="foo", or --agents-dir DIR into the CLI's agents_dir argument) has no coverage.
findings.impact: A typo or refactor in main()'s argument-to-overrides plumbing (e.g. swapping which override key a flag maps to, or dropping args.agents_dir from the build_plan(...) call) would not be caught by any test, even though the underlying build_plan/resolve_model behavior it depends on is otherwise well tested.
findings.remediation: Add a CLI-level test invoking dispatch.main([profile_path, "--host", "kimi", "--model-advisor", "custom", "--out", out_path]) and asserting the written plan's advisor entry uses the override model, plus a similar test for --agents-dir driving the `enforced` flag through main() rather than build_plan() directly.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified by exhaustive grep. skill/scripts/dispatch.py:363-367 declares --agents-dir, --model-lens-sweep, --model-panel-review, --model-advisor; lines 408-414 build the `overrides` dict from the three model flags and line 417-418 passes `agents_dir=args.agents_dir` into build_plan. I grepped the entire tests/ tree for `dispatch.main(` and got exactly eight call sites, all in tests/test_dispatch.py (lines 110, 123, 134, 154, 170, 318, 473, 478). Their argv lists use only: profile path, --host, --out, --render-advisor, --emit-host-agents. None passes --agents-dir or any --model-* flag. Every test that exercises overrides or agents_dir goes through the Python API instead: agents_dir=d at lines 93, 245, 394, 402, 412, and model overrides only via model_resolver.resolve_model directly (tests/test_model_resolver.py:30-32, 41-49). A repo-wide grep for the flag strings finds them only in dispatch.py, planning/spec docs, skill/SKILL.md, and tests/test_skill_md.py:55 — where '--agents-dir' is checked as a documentation TOKEN in SKILL.md prose, not as CLI behavior. tests/test_dispatch_integration.py and tests/test_e2e.py contain no dispatch CLI invocation with these flags either. So the argparse-to-overrides/agents_dir plumbing in main() is genuinely uncovered, exactly as claimed, and a swapped override key or a dropped args.agents_dir would go unnoticed. Two corrections for the auditor, neither of which changes the verdict: (1) the claim's suggested remediation of asserting 'the written plan's advisor entry uses the override model' is not implementable as written — build_plan never emits an advisor entry (dispatch.py:249-302 emits only panel_review and lens_sweep; tests/test_dispatch.py:94-95 asserts len(advisor)==0), so overrides['advisor'] set at dispatch.py:414 is currently plumbing that no consumer reads. That makes --model-advisor untested AND unused, arguably strengthening the coverage point. A workable test would assert --model-panel-review/--model-lens-sweep instead. (2) I checked whether the string-vs-dict shape of the CLI overrides was itself a latent bug: it is not — model_resolver.resolve_model handles a bare string override via `return {"model": override}` (model_resolver.py:106-110). Severity LOW is appropriate; this is a coverage gap, not a defect.

findings.title: agent_provenance(confirmed=True) and merge_provenance's model-less-expansion branch are untested
findings.description: test_agent_provenance_unconfirmed only calls pv.agent_provenance(role, model, version) with the default confirmed=False, so the `confirmation_status = "CONFIRMED" if confirmed else "UNVERIFIED"` branch for confirmed=True (provenance.py line 25) has no test. Similarly, test_merge_provenance_expansion only builds `expansion` via agent_provenance(...) with a truthy model, so merge_provenance's `if expansion.get("model")` guard (provenance.py lines 35-37) is only exercised on its true branch; the false branch -- where merged['model']/['model_version'] must remain equal to base's, e.g. when expansion is a tool_provenance() dict whose model is always None -- is never exercised.
findings.impact: A regression that flips the confirmed=True output value, or one that incorrectly overwrites/loses base's model fields when the expansion carries no model, would not be caught by the existing test suite.
findings.remediation: Add a test asserting agent_provenance(role, model, version, confirmed=True)['confirmation_status'] == 'CONFIRMED', and a merge_provenance test where the expansion dict has no 'model' key (or model=None, mirroring tool_provenance()'s shape) and asserts merged['model'] equals base's original model.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. skill/scripts/provenance.py:17-27 defines agent_provenance(role, model, model_version, confirmed=False) with the ternary at line 25 ('CONFIRMED' if confirmed else 'UNVERIFIED'), and merge_provenance (lines 30-38) guards the model/model_version overwrite with `if expansion.get("model")`. tests/test_provenance.py contains exactly three tests: test_tool_provenance (line 10), test_agent_provenance_unconfirmed (line 17, which calls pv.agent_provenance with three positional args and asserts confirmation_status == 'UNVERIFIED'), and test_merge_provenance_expansion (line 23, whose expansion is agent_provenance('panel_review', 'kimi-k3', 'v2') -- a truthy model, so only the true branch of line 35 runs; the assertion at line 29 is merged['model'] == 'kimi-k3'). A repo-wide grep for agent_provenance/merge_provenance/tool_provenance shows the only call sites are tests/test_provenance.py, skill/scripts/tools/base.py + sarif_utils.py (tool_provenance only), and a design doc; agent_provenance and merge_provenance have no production callers at all, and no test anywhere passes confirmed=True or a model-less expansion dict. tests/tools/test_base.py and tests/tools/test_legacy_sarif.py exercise only attach_tool_provenance/tool_provenance. So both cited branches are genuinely uncovered, as claimed. Two contextual notes that keep this at the claimed LOW/INFO end: (a) the uncovered branches are one-line, side-effect-free expressions; (b) since neither function is called by production code today, the regression risk is latent rather than active. The claim's technical assertions are nonetheless accurate as stated.

findings.title: The only regression test for the SEC-101 HTML-injection fix in _render_provenance checks cosmetic normalization, not adversarial input
findings.description: html_report.py:313-315 carries a comment: 'SEC-101: agent-authored value; restrict the class token to a safe charset instead of interpolating it raw into the HTML attribute', guarding `status_class = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9-]", "-", status.lower()) or "unknown"` for provenance.confirmation_status (an agent-authored, therefore untrusted, value). The only test exercising this sanitizer, test_provenance_needs_more_info_class_is_hyphenated, supplies confirmation_status='NEEDS_MORE_INFO' and asserts the benign underscore-to-hyphen mapping ('prov-needs-more-info' present, 'prov-needs_more_info' absent). No test in the file supplies an actually adversarial confirmation_status (e.g. containing `'`, `"`, `<`, `>`, or a value crafted to break out of the `class='prov-status prov-<token>'` attribute) to confirm the sanitizer neutralizes the injection this fix was written to prevent.
findings.impact: Since agent-authored provenance.confirmation_status values feed directly into an HTML class attribute, a future refactor of _render_provenance's sanitization regex (or its removal) that reintroduces the SEC-101 HTML-injection vulnerability would not be caught by any existing test -- the current test only verifies a cosmetic normalization detail, not the security property.
findings.remediation: Add a regression test that sets provenance.confirmation_status to an adversarial string (e.g. "foo'><script>alert(1)</script>") and asserts the rendered output contains no unescaped `<script`, `'`, or `>` inside the class attribute, directly exercising the property SEC-101 fixed.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every element checks out. (1) The guarded code exists verbatim: skill/scripts/html_report.py:313-315 carries the comment 'SEC-101: agent-authored value; restrict the class token to a safe charset instead of interpolating it raw into the HTML attribute' above `status_class = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9-]", "-", status.lower()) or "unknown"`, and line 318 interpolates it as `<span class='prov-status prov-{status_class}'>`, i.e. into a single-quoted HTML attribute. (2) The input really is untrusted along a reachable path: `confirmation_status` is agent-authored (skill/agents/lens-sweep.md:47, skill/agents/panel-review.md:51 both instruct agents to emit it). synthesize.normalize_finding (skill/scripts/synthesize.py:47-85) does not touch `provenance` at all, load_findings only strips `source`/`reinforced` (AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS, line 93), and validate_report (lines 716-755) checks id/title/category/severity/confidence/panel/evidence.status but never provenance.confirmation_status — so although report-schema.json:128-131 declares an enum, nothing in the render path enforces it, and the value flows straight to _render_provenance. Only evidence.apply_verdict (skill/scripts/evidence.py:232) constrains it, and only when an advisor verdict exists. (3) The test coverage gap is real: three tests reach _render_provenance — test_finding_card_renders_provenance ('TOOL', line 362), test_unverified_findings_render_separately / test_provenance_needs_more_info_class_is_hyphenated ('NEEDS_MORE_INFO', lines 381 and 400), and test_rejected_badge_has_distinct_style ('REJECTED', line 531) — and all four values are already within the safe charset apart from the underscore. Only test_provenance_needs_more_info_class_is_hyphenated (394-411) asserts on the sanitizer's output, and its assertions ('prov-needs-more-info' in, 'prov-needs_more_info' not in) are satisfied by any underscore-to-hyphen transform; removing the `[^a-z0-9-]` restriction in favour of `str.replace("_", "-")` would keep the whole suite green while restoring the injection. I grepped for quote/angle-bracket/script payloads across the file: the only adversarial inputs anywhere are `<script>alert('x')</script>` for _escape (line 65), `<script>` in meta.target (line 78), and `"CRITICAL<script>"` for _severity_class (line 425) — notably the analogous severity sanitizer DOES have an adversarial test, which the provenance one lacks. Repo-wide grep shows html_report is exercised only by tests/test_html_report.py; tests/test_synthesize.py mentions confirmation_status only with enum values (CONFIRMED/TOOL/UNVERIFIED) and its HTML tests (968-1059) only assert on file existence and '<!DOCTYPE html>'. Confidence is LIKELY rather than CERTAIN only because this is a test-design (missing-regression-test) claim, not a live defect: the current sanitizer is correct, so nothing is exploitable today.

findings.title: pip-audit/npm-audit integration tests make live network calls to third-party services with no opt-out marker
findings.description: test_pip_audit_finds_requests_cve, test_npm_audit_finds_lodash_vulnerability, and test_ingest_dir_routes_adapter_output invoke the real `pip-audit` / `npm audit` binaries against fixture manifests when those tools are installed. Both tools query live external vulnerability databases (PyPI's advisory feed / the npm registry) over the network; the adapters set a 300-second timeout (skill/scripts/tools/base.run_tool). The tests do gracefully skip when the binary is missing (FileNotFoundError) or returns an unexpected exit code, but there is no explicit network-availability check, no mock/cassette for the HTTP layer, and no test marker (e.g. a custom `@unittest.skipUnless(os.environ.get(...))`) allowing these tests to be excluded in an offline/air-gapped CI runner where the binaries are present but egress is blocked.
findings.impact: In an environment where pip-audit/npm are installed but network egress is restricted, these tests can hang for up to the full 300-second timeout per test before failing or skipping, rather than failing fast, making the suite slow and its failures indistinguishable from a genuine code defect without inspecting stderr. The tests are also inherently non-deterministic: results depend on the live state of PyPI/npm advisory databases at run time, not on pinned fixture data.
findings.remediation: Gate these three tests behind an explicit opt-in environment variable or pytest marker (e.g. skip unless PANOPTICON_NETWORK_TESTS=1), and/or reduce the adapter timeout used in tests specifically, so offline/CI runs fail fast and predictably rather than depending on live network reachability.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every structural element of the claim checks out. (1) The three named tests do invoke real binaries: test_pip_audit_finds_requests_cve (tests/test_phase1_integration.py:13-26) calls ADAPTERS['pip-audit'].invoke(target) on tests/fixtures/vulnerable-python (which contains a real requirements.txt pinning requests==2.25.1); test_npm_audit_finds_lodash_vulnerability (28-41) calls the npm-audit adapter on tests/fixtures/vulnerable-node (real package.json + package-lock.json pinning lodash 4.17.20); test_ingest_dir_routes_adapter_output (95-107) calls pip-audit's invoke again. (2) The invocations are unmocked shell-outs to network-backed scanners: skill/scripts/tools/pip_audit.py:27-42 builds ['pip-audit','--format=json','--desc=on', '--requirement', <req>] and skill/scripts/tools/npm_audit.py:16-18 builds ['npm','audit','--json','--prefix',target]. Neither passes any offline/cache/no-deps flag, and both resolve advisories from live services (PyPI/OSV advisory feed and the npm registry audit endpoint). (3) The 300-second timeout is real: both call run_tool(cmd, timeout=300), and skill/scripts/tools/base.py:64-78 passes that straight into subprocess.run(timeout=timeout). (4) The absence of any opt-out seam is verifiable and total: Glob found no conftest.py and no pytest.ini anywhere in the repo, a grep for skipUnless/pytest.mark/addopts across tests/ returned no gating for these tests, and .github/workflows/ci.yml runs `python -m pytest tests/ -q` with no marker filter. There is no HTTP mock/cassette for the adapter layer, even though the codebase demonstrates it knows the pattern elsewhere (tests/test_citations.py:135-140 injects a fake `opener` to simulate 'offline'), and a fixture-gating precedent exists at tests/tools/test_ruby_integration.py:8-10 (FIXTURE_ROOT env var + skipTest). I found evidence that strengthens the claim beyond what it states: subprocess.TimeoutExpired is caught nowhere — not in run_tool, not in the tests, which only catch FileNotFoundError — so a stalled connection surfaces as a hard test ERROR after 300s, not a skip; and test_ingest_dir_routes_adapter_output is the weakest of the three because it neither calls is_applicable() nor inspects the return code before asserting `self.assertTrue(findings)`, so a pip-audit run that fails for network reasons but still exits cleanly with an empty/partial payload fails the assertion rather than skipping. Note also that ubuntu-latest GitHub runners ship npm, so the npm-audit test really does perform a live registry audit in CI today (pip-audit is not in the CI pip install list, so those two skip there). One caveat holds my confidence at LIKELY rather than CERTAIN: whether a blocked-egress host actually burns the full 300s depends on the failure mode — DNS failure or connection refused fails in seconds, while a packet-dropping firewall does hang to the timeout. The core assertions (live third-party network dependency, no opt-out marker, results dependent on live advisory-database state rather than pinned fixture data) are certain; only the worst-case latency figure is environment-dependent. CWE-710 in the claim is a real CWE ('Improper Adherence to Coding Standards') but a weak fit for a test-hygiene issue; I have not carried it forward as verified.

findings.title: Resource leak: unclosed file handle in json.load(open(...))
findings.description: Line 83 uses json.load(open(...)) without a context manager. The file handle is never explicitly closed, causing a resource leak. This violates Python best practices and can lead to 'too many open files' errors in resource-constrained environments or when running many test iterations.
findings.impact: File handle resources are not properly released, which can accumulate and cause resource exhaustion. This is particularly problematic in CI/CD environments with repeated test runs.
findings.remediation: Use a context manager to ensure proper resource cleanup. Replace: schema = json.load(open(os.path.join(REF, "report-schema.json"), encoding="utf-8")) with: with open(os.path.join(REF, "report-schema.json"), encoding="utf-8") as fh: schema = json.load(fh)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The code fact is exactly as claimed. tests/test_schemas.py:83 reads `schema = json.load(open(os.path.join(REF, "report-schema.json"), encoding="utf-8"))` with no context manager, inside `TestAdapterFindingsValidateAgainstSchema._finding_schema`. This is a genuine inconsistency within the same file: the two sibling helpers `TestSchemas._load` (line 19) and `TestToolEvidenceSchema._load` (line 57) both use `with open(...) as fh: return json.load(fh)`, so the suggested remediation matches the file's own established idiom and is correct as written. I confirm the defect but the auditor should downgrade the stated impact, which I could not substantiate: on CPython (the only interpreter this project targets — pyproject.toml requires-python >=3.11 and .github/workflows/ci.yml runs the 3.11/3.12/3.13 matrix), the anonymous file object's refcount drops to zero the moment `json.load` returns, so the descriptor is released deterministically at that point. `_finding_schema` is also called only via `_validate`, i.e. roughly eight times per test run, so 'too many open files' / resource exhaustion in CI is not a reachable outcome. CWE-775 ('Missing Release of File Descriptor or Handle after Effective Lifetime') is therefore a poor fit, since release does occur at end of lifetime. Note also that nothing currently flags this automatically: pyproject.toml `[tool.ruff.lint]` selects only E, F, W, so the rule that would catch it (SIM115) is not enabled. Treat this as a LOW-severity style/consistency nit, not a resource leak.

findings.title: Fragile sys.path manipulation pattern duplicated across all 35 test files
findings.description: All test files use the same boilerplate `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir, 'skill'))` pattern to add the parent directory to Python path. This pattern is not maintainable and violates DRY principle.
findings.impact: Code duplication makes it harder to maintain test infrastructure. If the project structure changes, 35 files must be updated. No centralized way to manage import paths.
findings.remediation: Create a conftest.py file in the tests/ directory with a pytest fixture or use automatic sys.path configuration. This is Python testing standard practice.

findings.title: Multiple duplicate test helper factory functions across test suite
findings.description: Test helper functions like _entry() (test_verdict_ingest.py:11), _finding() (test_verify_queue.py:11), and _f() (test_synthesize.py:807) follow the same pattern but are duplicated across files with inconsistent names and minor implementation differences. The same pattern appears in test_evidence.py and multiple other test classes.
findings.impact: Maintenance burden: changes to the factory pattern must be replicated across multiple files. Inconsistency makes it harder for developers to understand test setup patterns.
findings.remediation: Consolidate all test factory functions into a shared test utilities module (e.g., tests/utils.py) or conftest.py. This centralizes test data generation and ensures consistency.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every cited location exists and the duplication is real. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_verdict_ingest.py:11-17 `_entry(fid, queue_id, **kw)` builds a finding dict then wraps it in {queue_id, priority, finding}. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_verify_queue.py:11-16 `_finding(fid, sev, **kw)` builds the identical base dict minus 'references'. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_evidence.py:9-15 `_finding(**kw)` builds the same base plus 'citation_quality'. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_synthesize.py:807-813 `_f(self, fid, panel, category, line, ...)` builds the same base with a positional signature. All four share the same key set (id, title, severity, confidence, panel, category, location{file,line_start}) and the same `f.update(kw); return f` shape, differing only in name, signature style, defaults and one or two extra keys -- exactly the 'inconsistent names and minor implementation differences' the claim describes. The pattern recurs three more times inside test_synthesize.py alone (`_f` at 256, `_finding` at 287, `_agentic` at 1106, `_f` at 1555) and once in test_html_report.py (`_minimal_report` at 10). The remediation is actionable because no shared location exists yet: a repo-wide glob for conftest.py returns no files, and there is no tests/utils.py. The duplicated shape is a genuine cross-module contract (defined in skill/reference/report-schema.json), which is what makes a single shared factory sensible rather than arbitrary. Two caveats for the auditor: MEDIUM severity is inflated for test-only helper duplication with no runtime or security exposure -- LOW is the honest grade; and the helpers are not strictly interchangeable today (test_verify_queue.py's takes fid/sev positionally, test_verdict_ingest.py's returns a queue envelope rather than a bare finding), so consolidation is a real refactor, not a mechanical move.

findings.title: Inline test double classes repeated throughout test_run_tools.py
findings.description: Multiple inline class definitions (e.g., `class R:` at lines 15, 23, 49, 58, 74, 108, 127, 143) are defined inside test methods as single-use mocks/stubs. Each instance is a minimal test double with properties like returncode, stdout, stderr, or name. These should be centralized into a test doubles module.
findings.impact: Code duplication and reduced readability. Test doubles are harder to discover and reuse. The same pattern could be applied consistently with named classes in a fixtures module.
findings.remediation: Extract inline class definitions into a test doubles/fixtures module (e.g., tests/test_doubles.py or tests/fixtures.py). Define named classes like FakeResult, FakeAdapter, etc. Import and reuse them in tests.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The factual content checks out. A grep for `class R\b|class Fake` in `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_run_tools.py` returns 12 inline class definitions nested inside test methods: `class R` at lines 15, 22, 49, 58, 74, 108, 127, 143 (eight, exactly the count claimed), `class FakeAdapter` at 90, 102, 174, and `class FakeOut` at 181. The duplication is literal, not just structural: lines 58, 127 and 143 are byte-identical (`class R: returncode = 0; stdout = b'{"runs":[]}'; stderr = b''`), line 74 is the same body indented one level deeper inside a runner closure, and 108 differs only in the stdout payload. The three `FakeAdapter` definitions likewise differ only in `invoke`'s return payload and whether `is_applicable` is present. The claim's line list has one off-by-one -- the second `class R` is on line 22, not 23 (line 23 is its `returncode = 1` body) -- but the claim's own cited location range is 15-24, which spans it, so this is a transcription slip rather than a wrong claim. Judgment: this is a style/maintainability observation, not a defect; the inline doubles are locally readable and keep each test self-contained, and a reasonable reviewer could argue that centralizing them into tests/test_doubles.py would trade locality for indirection. But the claim does not overstate -- it is filed LOW, describes the code accurately, and the proposed remediation is a legitimate option. findings.title: Bare, unscoped `# noqa` applied inconsistently to identical fake-response classes
findings.description: tests/test_run_tools.py defines the same throwaway fake-response pattern (`class R: ...` carrying `returncode`/`stdout`/`stderr`) eight times across the file. Only the first two occurrences (lines 15 and 22) carry a bare `# noqa` comment; the other six structurally-identical occurrences (lines 49, 58, 74, 108, 127, 143) carry no noqa at all. The project's ruff config (pyproject.toml `[tool.ruff.lint]`) already globally ignores E701/E702 (the "multiple statements on one line" rules a `class R: attr = val` one-liner would trigger), so none of these eight declarations actually need suppression - making the two bare `# noqa` comments vestigial. Elsewhere in this same suite (tests/test_synthesize.py:1482) the project follows the safer convention of a scoped `# noqa: E402`, naming the specific rule being suppressed.
findings.impact: A bare `# noqa` silently suppresses every lint rule on that line, not just the one presumably intended, which can mask a genuinely new lint violation introduced later on the same line. The 2-of-8 inconsistency also suggests copy/paste drift rather than an intentional suppression.
findings.remediation: Remove the now-unnecessary bare `# noqa` on lines 15 and 22, or replace it with a scoped `# noqa: <code>` matching the convention already used at test_synthesize.py:1482.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified each factual component. tests/test_run_tools.py declares a throwaway fake-response `class R` exactly eight times, at lines 15, 22, 49, 58, 74, 108, 127, 143. A repo-wide grep for 'noqa' in *.py confirms only lines 15 and 22 carry `class R:  # noqa` (bare, unscoped); the other six carry none. pyproject.toml [tool.ruff.lint] is `select = ["E", "F", "W"]` with `ignore = ["E401", "E501", "E701", "E702"]`, so E701/E702 are globally ignored and none of the eight declarations needs suppression -- making the two bare `# noqa` comments vestigial. The scoped-convention counterexample is real: tests/test_synthesize.py:1482 reads `import scripts.evidence as evidence_mod  # noqa: E402`, and skill/scripts/ uses scoped `# noqa: BLE001` in eight places. CI does lint tests/ (`python -m ruff check skill/scripts/ tests/` in .github/workflows/ci.yml), so the suppressions are live, not dead config. One correction to the claim's wording, which does not change the verdict and in fact strengthens it: lines 15 and 22 are NOT structurally identical to the other six -- they are two-line class bodies (`class R:` / `returncode = 0`) that could never trigger E701/E702, whereas the six un-suppressed ones are the actual `class R: returncode = 2; stdout = ...; stderr = ...` one-liners. So the noqa is present precisely where it can accomplish nothing and absent where the ignored rules would have fired. The impact statement (a bare noqa suppresses all rules on the line) is correct per ruff's error-suppression semantics. INFO severity is appropriate.

findings.title: Imports inside test methods instead of at module level
findings.description: Multiple test methods import modules inside their function bodies (line 214: `import tempfile`, line 201: `import contextlib, io`) instead of declaring them at the module level. This appears in test_synthesize.py and other test files.
findings.impact: Reduces readability and violates Python style conventions (PEP 8). Import statements at the top of a file make dependencies clear. Late imports can also introduce subtle bugs if imports fail during test execution.
findings.remediation: Move all import statements to the top of the module. The fact that some are already there (line 1-8) while others are inside methods is inconsistent and should be normalized.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The general assertion holds but both pieces of cited evidence are wrong, so this needs correction before it is actionable. Wrong parts: line 214 of tests/test_synthesize.py is a comment (`# confidence is never mutated by the pipeline (amended spec) -- the`) inside test_reinforce_sourceless_agent_with_tool, not `import tempfile`; line 201 is `findings = [`, not `import contextlib, io`. Grepping the whole file for `import tempfile` returns exactly one hit, line 6 at module scope -- there is no function-body `import tempfile` anywhere in the file, so that specific evidence is fabricated. Correct parts: function-body imports do exist, at lines 101 and 117 (`import contextlib, io`), 376, 419, 437, 525, 560, 646, 761 (`import io, contextlib`), 489-490 (`import io` / `import contextlib` on separate lines), and 1086 (`import scripts.dispatch as dispatch`). All of the contextlib/io ones are strictly redundant because contextlib and io are already imported at module lines 1-2, which makes the real defect 'redundant shadowing re-imports' rather than the claim's framing of 'dependencies not declared at the top'; the remediation as written ('move all import statements to the top') is therefore slightly off -- the fix is to delete them. Also note there is a legitimate counter-case the claim sweeps in: line 1482 carries `import scripts.evidence as evidence_mod  # noqa: E402`, a deliberate mid-file import with an explicit lint suppression, and line 1086's `import scripts.dispatch` is a local import of a sibling script that depends on the sys.path mutation at line 9. The claim's stated impact ('can introduce subtle bugs if imports fail during test execution') is not substantiated -- these are stdlib modules already loaded at module scope. The repo's own linter would not flag these either: pyproject.toml selects ruff rules E, F, W and explicitly ignores E401 (multiple imports on one line), and PLC0415 (import-outside-top-level) is not in the selected set. Confirming on substance at LOW severity, with the line numbers and the `import tempfile` example corrected.

findings.title: Redundant local re-imports of io/contextlib shadow module-level imports
findings.description: Nine test methods in tests/test_synthesize.py locally re-import `io` and/or `contextlib` (lines 101, 117, 376, 419, 437, 525, 560, 646, 761) even though both modules are already imported once at the top of the file (lines 1-2: `import contextlib` / `import io`). findings.title: test_synthesize.py is a single 1,736-line module covering ~27 unrelated test-suite concerns
findings.description: tests/test_synthesize.py contains roughly 27 distinct TestCase classes spanning normalization, dedupe, grading, report building, CLI argument handling, cross-panel corroboration, HTML rendering/compare, evidence-gate semantics, fingerprinting, and tool-finding aggregation - a much broader surface than the file's name ("test_synthesize") suggests, and far larger than sibling files that already split related concerns into their own files (e.g. tests/test_evidence.py, tests/test_provenance.py, tests/test_citations.py).
findings.impact: The size makes the file harder to navigate, slows targeted test runs/greps against a single concern, and increases the chance of unrelated changes causing merge conflicts in the same file.
findings.remediation: Split the file along the lines the class names already suggest (e.g. test_synthesize_dedupe.py, test_synthesize_report.py, test_synthesize_cross_panel.py, test_synthesize_html.py), following the precedent already set by test_evidence.py / test_provenance.py / test_citations.py.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The measurable core of the claim checks out, but two of its supporting arguments do not. VERIFIED: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_synthesize.py is 1,735 lines (ripgrep line count; the claim's 1,736 is off by one, immaterial) and contains 28 top-level `unittest.TestCase` classes (claim says ~27). It is by far the largest file in the suite -- the next largest are tests/test_html_report.py at 552 lines and tests/test_dispatch.py at 488, so it is roughly 3x the next biggest. Signs of accretion are visible in-file: a module-level helper `_agentic()` defined mid-file at line 1106, and a mid-file module-level import at line 1482 (`import scripts.evidence as evidence_mod  # noqa: E402`) that needed a lint suppression to live there. Two classes genuinely reach outside the module under test: TestGroupReMatchesDispatchNames (line 1084, imports scripts.dispatch at line 1086) and TestEvidenceIntegrity (line 1485, drives scripts.evidence). NOT SUPPORTED: the framing that the ~27 concerns are 'unrelated' and 'a much broader surface than the file's name suggests'. Nearly every class exercises skill/scripts/synthesize.py (998 lines -- the largest script in skill/scripts/), which is exactly what a file named test_synthesize.py should cover. TestHtmlOut (line 967) tests syn.main's --html-out/--compare CLI wiring, not html_report internals (those live in tests/test_html_report.py against scripts.html_report). The cited 'precedent' is also inaccurate: tests/test_evidence.py, tests/test_provenance.py and tests/test_citations.py each map 1:1 to a separate source module (scripts/evidence.py, scripts/provenance.py, scripts/citations.py) -- they are per-module files, not a per-concern split of one module's tests, so they do not establish the precedent the remediation leans on. Net: the file is genuinely oversized and splitting it is a defensible LOW-severity maintainability suggestion, but the auditor should discard the 'unrelated concerns' and precedent reasoning when writing this up.

findings.title: Fixture manifest drives supply-chain-unsafe, unpinned third-party code execution during image build
findings.description: tests/fixtures/manifest.json declares the fixtures (railsgoat, WebGoat, AspGoat, vulnerable-rust) that Dockerfile.fixtures fetches and builds to validate panopticon's scanner adapters. Cross-referencing the manifest with Dockerfile.fixtures (build-time consumer of this data) shows two of the four sources are cloned from a floating `main` branch rather than a pinned commit SHA or release tag: `ARG RAILS_GOAT_REF=main` (github.com/OWASP/railsgoat) and `ARG ASP_GOAT_REF=main` (github.com/Soham7-dev/AspGoat). The AspGoat source is additionally an individual/unofficial GitHub account rather than a vetted security-org repo, unlike the other three fixtures. After cloning, the Dockerfile actively builds this untrusted, unpinned code as root (`USER root`): `dotnet restore && dotnet build` for AspGoat, `bundle install` for railsgoat, `mvn clean compile` for WebGoat. `dotnet restore`/NuGet, Bundler, and Maven all support build-time code execution via package install scripts / MSBuild targets / Maven plugins. manifest.json itself has no field to express or audit a pinned ref, which is what allowed the consumer to default to a mutable branch.
findings.impact: Anyone building the fixtures image (`docker build -f Dockerfile.fixtures ...`, documented as the normal workflow for validating adapters) fetches and executes whatever code currently sits on `Soham7-dev/AspGoat`'s or `OWASP/railsgoat`'s default branch at build time. A takeover of the low-visibility personal AspGoat account, or a malicious merge to either project's main branch, achieves arbitrary code execution as root inside the build environment of contributors (and any CI job that ever builds this Dockerfile), with no way for panopticon to detect or roll back to a known-good version because no commit is pinned.
findings.remediation: Add a `ref`/`commit` field to each manifest.json fixture entry and require Dockerfile.fixtures to consume it (no default of `main`). Pin railsgoat and AspGoat to specific commit SHAs, verified once and updated deliberately. Prefer an OWASP-maintained or otherwise vetted equivalent over the unaudited personal AspGoat fork, or vendor/mirror a reviewed snapshot. Avoid running the fixture build as root beyond what OS package installation strictly requires, and keep the fixtures image isolated from secrets/credentials.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker gains commit access to (or already controls, in the case of the low-visibility personal fork) Soham7-dev/AspGoat's `main` branch and adds a malicious NuGet package reference or MSBuild target with a pre-build execution hook. The next time a panopticon contributor runs `docker build -f Dockerfile.fixtures -t panopticon-fixtures:latest .` to validate the roslyn-secguard adapter (a documented, routine workflow), `dotnet restore && dotnet build` executes the attacker's payload as root inside the build context, without any commit-pin mismatch to alert the operator.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion in the claim is verifiable in the repo. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/Dockerfile.fixtures line 6 sets `USER root` and never drops back; lines 25-32 clone three third-party repos, two of them from a floating default branch (`ARG RAILS_GOAT_REF=main` -> github.com/OWASP/railsgoat.git, `ARG ASP_GOAT_REF=main` -> github.com/Soham7-dev/AspGoat.git). Only WebGoat carries a ref (`ARG WEB_GOAT_REF=v2023.8`, a tag, not a SHA — still movable, but a materially smaller drift window). Lines 35-37 then execute build tooling over that freshly-cloned, unpinned code as root: `bundle install`, `./mvnw clean compile` / `mvn clean compile`, and `dotnet restore && dotnet build`. Bundler Gemfile evaluation, Maven plugin execution, and NuGet/MSBuild restore targets are all build-time code-execution surfaces, so a malicious commit on either `main` branch reaches root-level execution inside the build. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/fixtures/manifest.json does record `source` per fixture but has no `ref`/`commit` field, and skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py only reads `name`, `language`, and `path` from it — so nothing in the manifest can express or audit a pin, exactly as claimed. The AspGoat source is indeed an individual account (Soham7-dev) rather than a vetted security org, and the design spec (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-02-local-scanner-fixture-suite-design.md:190) explicitly treats pinning as 'optional for extra stability' — i.e., the risk was never accepted on security grounds, only deferred on stability grounds. Two corrections to the claim's impact framing that the auditor should carry forward, neither of which negates the finding: (1) 'any CI job that ever builds this Dockerfile' is not currently realized — no workflow builds Dockerfile.fixtures; .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml is scoped to the main `Dockerfile` and skill/scripts paths only, and ci.yml/security.yml/codeql.yml do not reference it. The exposure today is contributor workstations invoking the documented `docker build -f Dockerfile.fixtures ...` (DEVELOPMENT.md:78) or `run_fixture_tests.py --rebuild`. (2) The CVSS 8.1 AV:N/S:C looks inflated for a local-only, opt-in dev image whose own comment (Dockerfile.fixtures:54-55) says 'intended for local test use only'; MEDIUM-to-HIGH is the defensible band. Related but unclaimed, and worth folding into the same remediation: Dockerfile.fixtures:16 pipes an unpinned remote script to a root shell with no checksum — `RUN curl -sfL https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh | bash -s -- --channel 8.0` — which is a more direct instance of the same weakness class than either git clone.

findings.title: Tool/adapter stderr is silently discarded whenever the process exits 0/1, hiding scan failures behind a 'clean' result (detection-evasion vector)
findings.description: Reading the production code these tests pin down: `skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py::main()` catches any exception thrown by `adapter.invoke(target)`, prints a diagnostic + full traceback to stderr, and returns rc=0 (asserted by `test_main_skips_adapter_that_crashes`, line 198-209). Separately, `test_run_tools_skips_tool_on_unexpected_returncode` (line 46-54) shows that only a returncode OUTSIDE {0,1} triggers a stderr warning from `run_tools.run_tools()`; rc 0/1 is treated as the unconditional 'happy path'. Reading `skill/scripts/run_tools.py` (lines 132-176) confirms the resulting gap directly: on the rc-in-(0,1) branch for BOTH the legacy tool path and the Phase-1 adapter-dispatch path, the code writes `res.stdout` to the output file and appends to `written`, but never inspects or surfaces `res.stderr` -- it is captured via `subprocess.PIPE` and then dropped. The two behaviors compose: an adapter that crashes mid-parse writes its crash traceback only to the disposable container's stderr, exits 0, and the orchestrating process discards that stderr entirely because rc=0 is the 'success' branch.
findings.impact: A target repository containing a file that reliably crashes a specific SAST/SCA adapter's parser (a malformed lockfile, an edge-case syntax construct, etc.) causes that tool's entire contribution to the scan to silently vanish -- no warning reaches the synthesized report or CI logs, and the pipeline behaves identically to 'the tool ran and found nothing'. This is a realistic detection-evasion technique against panopticon's own tool layer: real vulnerabilities that only the crashed tool would have caught are missed with no visible signal to the analyst relying on the report.
findings.remediation: Surface `res.stderr` (or at least its last N bytes) to the operator/report whenever a tool or adapter's stdout output is empty or unexpectedly small, even on rc 0/1. Consider distinguishing 'clean' (rc=0, non-trivial parseable output) from 'crashed but exited 0' (rc=0, empty/garbage output) explicitly, and record a machine-readable 'tool_status: crashed' marker in the report's meta so downstream consumers can see which tools genuinely produced zero findings versus which silently failed.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every code-level assertion in this claim verifies against the source. (1) `/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py` lines 23-28: `try: stdout, rc = adapter.invoke(target) / except Exception as exc: print(f"adapter {name} crashed: {exc}; skipping", file=sys.stderr); traceback.print_exc(file=sys.stderr); return 0`. A crashing adapter yields rc=0 with an empty stdout and the only record of the crash on stderr -- exactly what tests/test_run_tools.py:198-209 pins (`self.assertEqual(rc, 0)` for CrashingAdapter). (2) `skill/scripts/run_tools.py` legacy path, lines 133-144: `res = runner(docker, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, timeout=TOOL_TIMEOUT)`; the stderr excerpt is decoded and printed ONLY inside the `if getattr(res, 'returncode', 1) not in (0, 1)` branch (lines 135-141). On the rc-in-(0,1) branch the code goes straight to `fh.write(res.stdout or b"")` and `written.append(out_path)` -- `res.stderr` is captured via PIPE and then dropped without ever being read. (3) The Phase-1 adapter dispatch path, lines 169-176, is strictly worse than the legacy path: its non-(0,1) branch prints only `"adapter %s exited %s; skipping"` with NO stderr excerpt at all (line 172), and its rc-in-(0,1) branch again writes `res.stdout or b""` and never touches `res.stderr`. So the composition the claim describes is real: adapter crashes in-container -> traceback to container stderr -> exit 0 -> host discards that stderr and writes a zero-byte `<tool>.json`, which is then appended to `written` as though it were a successful scan. (4) The 'no machine-readable tool status' half also verifies: `synthesize.py` build_report's `"meta"` block (lines 678-686) carries only target/review_type/timestamp/version/security_mode/models_used/tool_policy_mode -- there is no per-tool status, no list of tools attempted vs. ingested, so a vanished tool is indistinguishable in the report from a tool that found nothing. A grep for `tools_run|tool_status|tools_used` across skill/ finds no such field anywhere. One nuance that narrows (but does not defeat) the claim's impact wording: in the specific zero-byte-file sub-case, `ingest_tools.ingest_dir` (skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:78-82) will call `adapter.parse(b'')`, which raises (e.g. pip_audit.py:50 `json.loads(raw.decode(...))` on empty input) and prints `"ingest error %s: %s"` to stderr -- so an operator watching CI stderr does get *a* signal at the ingest stage, just not the cause. The fully silent variant is the one the claim's threat model actually needs and which the code permits unconditionally: a scanner that exits 0 (or 1) emitting structurally valid but empty/partial output while writing its parse failures to stderr -- e.g. semgrep's per-file parse errors -- parses cleanly into zero findings, and its stderr is discarded by run_tools with no trace. Same gap is mirrored in `skill/scripts/tools/base.py:run_tool` (lines 72-78), which likewise surfaces the stderr excerpt only when `rc not in ok_codes`. CWE-390 (Detection of Error Condition Without Action) and CWE-778 (Insufficient Logging) are both real CWE entries and are the right mappings. MEDIUM severity is appropriate: no direct exploit primitive, but a genuine integrity gap in the scanner's own reporting path.

CWE-390 (Detection of Error Condition Without Action) and CWE-778 (Insufficient Logging) are both real CWE entries and are the right mappings. MEDIUM severity is appropriate: no direct exploit primitive, but a genuine integrity gap in the scanner's own reporting path.

findings.title: Advisor verdict ingestion trusts lenient, unauthenticated free-text LLM output that can silently suppress confirmed security findings
findings.description: `test_loads_verdict_wrapped_in_prose` (line 58-66) shows the verdict loader extracts a JSON object from anywhere inside an advisor's free-form prose response via regex, not a structured/strict format. `test_missing_echo_accepted_with_warning` (line 78-80) shows a verdict file lacking the `finding_id` echo field is still matched and applied to its queue entry (identity is derived only from the verdict file's *position* -- its queue-id filename -- with echo-matching as an optional, skippable extra check). Cross-referenced against `tests/test_synthesize.py::TestEvidenceReport.test_rejected_moves_to_discarded_with_severity_intact`, a `REJECTED` verdict unconditionally removes the finding from the report's `findings` list into `discarded_claims` -- i.e. a single piece of loosely-parsed LLM prose is sufficient to make a confirmed vulnerability disappear from the final human-facing report.
findings.impact: If the advisor sub-agent that produces verdicts is prompt-injected (e.g. by adversarial content embedded in the target repository it is asked to analyze, such as a comment or docstring engineered to look like advisor-authoring instructions), or if its output is otherwise manipulated, it can cause a real, otherwise-CONFIRMED vulnerability to be marked REJECTED and dropped from the report with no independent verification step. Because acceptance of a verdict tolerates missing echo fields and free-text wrapping, the bar for a spoofed/injected verdict to be accepted is low.
findings.remediation: Require the `finding_id` echo field to be present and matching before a verdict is applied (make the currently-optional check mandatory, with rejection -- not just a warning -- on mismatch or absence). Consider requiring a second independent confirmation (a different reviewer/model) before a REJECTED verdict fully removes a HIGH/CRITICAL finding from the report, rather than moving it to discarded_claims on a single verdict. Treat advisor output that isn't well-formed JSON (no fence, embedded in prose) as lower-trust and log/flag such verdicts distinctly in the report for human review.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The mechanism described is real and I verified every link in the chain. (1) Lenient parsing: skill/scripts/evidence.py:155-167 `load_json_tolerant` strips markdown fences and, on JSONDecodeError, falls back to `re.search(r"(\{.*\})", body, re.DOTALL)` — i.e. it extracts the first-to-last brace span from arbitrary prose. `load_verdicts` (evidence.py:170-199) routes every verdict file through it and keys the result by the FILENAME STEM only (line 198: `out[name[:-len('.json')]] = data`), so verdict identity is positional. (2) Optional echo: `match_verdict` (evidence.py:206-221) returns the verdict with only a stderr warning when `finding_id` is absent (`if echoed is None: print(...'accepting'); return v`); it only rejects on an explicit mismatch. Both cited tests accurately encode this behavior. (3) Consequence: skill/scripts/synthesize.py:623-648 applies the matched verdict, then `rejected = [f for f in findings if f['evidence']['status'] == 'rejected']` and `active = [...] != 'rejected'`; `gate_eligible` is derived from `active` in BOTH branches, so a REJECTED verdict removes the finding from `findings`, from grades, from risk_level, and from the CI gate even under `--gate-unverified`. Trust boundary is real: skill/SKILL.md:56-60 says the advisor RETURNS free text that the orchestrator writes verbatim to `.panopticon/verdicts/{queue_id}.json`, and skill/agents/advisor.md gives the advisor Read/Grep/Glob over the (potentially adversarial) target repo — so repo-embedded injection reaching advisor output is a plausible path, and nothing corroborates a single REJECTED verdict. TWO CORRECTIONS to the claim's framing that the auditor should carry forward: (a) 'disappear from the final human-facing report' is overstated — rejected findings are preserved verbatim in `report['discarded_claims']` (synthesize.py:700) with severity and advisor reasoning intact, are counted in `summary.evidence_stats` (evidence_stats is called over all `findings`, synthesize.py:696), and ARE rendered by skill/scripts/html_report.py:662-673/699 in a collapsed 'Discarded claims' section. The real loss is gate/grade suppression and demotion out of the main findings list, not deletion. (b) The proposed primary remediation (mandatory `finding_id` echo) does NOT mitigate the stated prompt-injection impact: skill/scripts/dispatch.py:345-346 embeds the entire claim JSON — including its `id` — into the advisor prompt, so an injected advisor trivially echoes the correct id. Only the corroboration requirement (second independent verdict for HIGH/CRITICAL rejections) and distinct flagging of non-well-formed verdict payloads would actually address it. Severity MEDIUM is defensible; note also that this leniency is a documented design choice (evidence.py docstrings; SKILL.md:121-122), so it is a trust-boundary/design gap rather than an implementation bug.

findings.title: Fixture-noise suppression exists only for tool/SARIF findings, not for LLM agent (lens_sweep/panel_review) findings, on the very files this reviewer was asked to analyze
findings.description: tests/fixtures/insecure-js/app.js (`eval(userInput)`), tests/fixtures/vulnerable-node/{package.json,package-lock.json} (lodash 4.17.20, CVE-2020-8203), and tests/fixtures/vulnerable-python/requirements.txt (requests==2.25.1, CVE-2023-32681) are intentionally-vulnerable calibration fixtures used to validate scanner adapters. `skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py::ingest_dir()` implements an explicit, documented exclusion mechanism (F-CAL-2, `exclude_globs=['tests/fixtures/*']`, used by `.github/workflows/security.yml`) specifically because 'intentionally vulnerable apps under tests/fixtures/ dominate self-scans otherwise'. That mechanism only filters findings that came from SARIF/tool adapters. No equivalent exists for LLM-authored lens_sweep/panel_review findings dispatched over the same paths -- confirmed by the fact that this very review group (`._8`) was dispatched these exact fixture files for agentic security analysis with no annotation marking them as intentional/expected.
findings.impact: Every agent-based panel_review/lens_sweep pass over this group will legitimately (and, from the agent's local view, correctly) flag the fixtures' intentional vulnerabilities as real defects. Unlike tool findings, these agent findings have no automatic suppression path, so they can reach the verify queue, receive a CONFIRMED verdict from an advisor unaware of fixture intent, and (under `--gate-unverified` or after confirmation) contribute to gate failures or report noise that is indistinguishable from a genuine regression -- undermining the signal-to-noise ratio of exactly the reports this pipeline exists to produce.
findings.remediation: Extend the F-CAL-2-style exclusion to the agent/dispatch layer: either exclude `tests/fixtures/**` from scope-profile group file selection for lens_sweep/panel_review dispatch by default, or inject explicit context into the relevant group's prompt (e.g. a `_fixture_context` note in dispatch metadata) telling agents these paths are known-intentional-vulnerable calibration fixtures so they can annotate findings accordingly instead of reporting them as live defects. At minimum, apply the existing `--exclude-globs` filtering to agent-sourced findings in synthesize.py's load/dedupe path, not just tool-sourced ones.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every structural assertion checks out. (1) The tool-side exclusion exists and is documented as claimed: skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py:40-50 defines `ingest_dir(tools_dir, group, exclude_globs=None)` with the F-CAL-2 docstring naming 'intentionally vulnerable apps under tests/fixtures/'; the filter at lines 83-91 matches fnmatch patterns against `f['location']['file']` of findings returned by `adapter.parse()` only. .github/workflows/security.yml:60-63 calls it with `exclude_globs=['tests/fixtures/*']`. tests/test_ingest_tools.py:204-228 covers it. (2) It is genuinely tool-only. In skill/scripts/synthesize.py, `--tools-exclude` (line 862) is passed to exactly one place, `ingest_tools.ingest_dir(..., exclude_globs=args.tools_exclude)` at line 938-939. Agent findings come from `load_findings(args.files)` at line 936, whose body (lines 96-134) applies AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS stripping and normalization but no path/glob filtering whatsoever. (3) No exclusion at the dispatch layer either: skill/scripts/orchestrator.py:21-36 (`EXCLUDE_DIRS`, `EXCLUDE_DIR_GLOBS`, `ALLOWED_DOTDIR_SUBTREES`) prunes VCS/venv/cache/tmp trees and contains no tests/fixtures entry; grepping skill/scripts/dispatch.py for 'fixture' returns nothing, so no `_fixture_context`-style annotation is injected. (4) The dispatch evidence is real: .panopticon.prev-20260803/scout-prompts/._8.md:85-98 lists group ._8's files including tests/fixtures/insecure-js/app.js, tests/fixtures/vulnerable-node/{package.json,package-lock.json} and tests/fixtures/vulnerable-python/requirements.txt, with no annotation of fixture intent. (5) The asymmetry reaches the verify queue as claimed: skill/scripts/evidence.py:92-120 `build_verify_queue` queues `not is_tool_sourced(f) and not f.get('reinforced')` -- i.e. by design tool findings are excluded and agentic ones are included (asserted by tests/test_verify_queue.py:36-41 `test_tools_excluded_agentic_included`). So an agent-authored fixture finding is filtered by neither mechanism and lands in front of an advisor. Corroborating independent evidence: the repo's own docs/superpowers/2026-08-04-run2-fixmes.md:48-59 records this identically as 'FIXME-4 -- No agent-side fixture exclusion' ('There is no equivalent for the agent path... Run 2 excluded group ._9 by hand, which is not a mechanism'), and docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-calibration-fixmes.md:79-83 flags the same gap. Two caveats an auditor should weigh, neither of which changes the verdict: the issue is already tracked internally, so it is a duplicate rather than a novel discovery; and I verified queue inclusion directly but did not trace the full `--gate-unverified` grading path, so the 'contributes to gate failures' half of the impact is inferred rather than line-verified. CWE-436 (interpretation conflict) is a loose fit for what is really a suppression-coverage gap.

findings.title: Non-zero exit code handling in run_adapters not fully tested
findings.description: Lines 104-106 handle adapter exit codes not in (0, 1) as errors, but test coverage only exercises returncode=0. The rc=1 case (valid for 'findings found') and rc>=2 cases are handled in code but never tested by test_run_adapters_writes_raw_output.
findings.impact: Silent failures if exit code handling logic is broken; tests would not catch regressions in error-handling paths.
findings.remediation: Add test cases for returncode=1 (valid findings) and returncode=2+ (errors) in run_adapters function.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Verified directly. `run_adapters` at /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/run_tools.py:94-112 has three behavioral branches: the success path (rc in (0,1) -> write file, append to `written`), the skip path at lines 104-106 (`if rc not in (0, 1): print(...); continue`), and the tolerant `except Exception` path at 110-111. The only test that calls `run_adapters` anywhere in the repo is tests/test_run_tools.py:89-99 (`test_run_adapters_writes_raw_output`), whose FakeAdapter returns `(b'{"results":[]}', 0)` — rc=0 only. I grepped for `run_adapters` repo-wide and for `run_tools` inside tests/: the only hits are the definition, that single test call, and docs/plan files. So the claim is factually correct: the rc-not-in-(0,1) branch and the exception branch of `run_adapters` are never exercised.

Two qualifications the auditor should weigh, neither of which contradicts the claim:
(1) The rc=1 case the claim asks to be tested is behaviorally identical to rc=0 (both fall through to the same `open(...)/write/append`), so a rc=1 test adds near-zero branch coverage; the real gaps are lines 104-106 and 110-111.
(2) The stated impact ("silent failures") is overstated because `run_adapters` has no production caller. `main` (lines 184-205) calls `run_tools`, not `run_adapters`, and `run_tools`'s adapter-dispatch branch (lines 152-180) reimplements the same logic independently — and that duplicate IS covered for the error case by tests/test_run_tools.py:46-54 (`test_run_tools_skips_tool_on_unexpected_returncode`, returncode=2). So the untested code is currently reachable only from tests. That argues the severity is LOW rather than MEDIUM, and that 'delete or wire up run_adapters' may be a better remediation than 'add tests'.
The CWE-1084 citation is carried as verified:false and does not map to a test-coverage weakness; it should not be relied on.
